#4482. This Chinese EV Maker Wants To Put A Foot Bath In The Back Seat Of Your Car. Really

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

If you've ever been in the back of a Rolls-Royce, you'll know just how lovely its rear lambswool carpets are. Their shag is so deep, soft, and luxurious that it's a crime to keep your shoes on back there. While enjoying them, you might think they're the pinnacle of rear seat foot comfort. However, Chinese EV maker Deepal wants to one-up even Rolls-Royce, with an extendable backseat foot bath.

According to Australia's Which Car?, Changan sub-brand Deepal recently filed a patent for a foot bath that would extend out from under the front seats, so that passengers can literally wash their feet while on the move. Once extended, rear passengers can place their feet in the water, which is presumably heated, and even massage them on rollers at the bottom of the basin. Hopefully, there's a towel rack or cubby back there, otherwise you're taking wet feet out and soaking the carpets, which sounds like a nightmare for interior mold.

What about sloshing? I can't even drive around with a Wawa coffee cup filled near the top or it'll slosh out of the spout onto my center console. So how is a basin of water not going to toss all of its water onto the floor at the first bump or turn? According to Car Expert, Deepal's patent claims that the basin can actually block the water from sloshing out. It also has guide holes which let sloshing water recirculate into the bottom, keeping the liquid level low.

There's also a disinfection assembly, to keep the water from being gross, and a quick disconnect to dispose of the water from the vehicle body.

Will this technology ever actually make production? Who knows, as automakers often patent wild ideas just to future-proof their ability to make it one day. But foot baths are quite popular in China, so who knows, maybe there's enough demand for this sort of thing. If it never makes production (which seems likely),though, I think some deep carpets and no shoes, Die Hard-style, will do just fine.

#4481. Too Much Motion in the Ocean: We Test the 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLS450

The revised GLS-class pushes luxury to the front of the line at the cost of some composure.

You can have the world’s best cartographers in your employ, and your ship can still end up drifting off course. The 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLS450 is one such boat. Mercedes has buildings full of nitpicky engineers whose sole collective life goal is to build the most comfortable three-row SUV on terra firma. And while the result of the GLS’s latest refresh largely hits the mark, we believe this ute’s ride quality missed its intended landing zone.

Let’s focus on the high points first. We’re big fans of the base GLS450’s 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-six. Thanks to a stronger electric supercharger and a few other updates, this powertrain now spits out 375 horsepower and 413 pound-feet of torque fed through a nine-speed automatic transmission to all four wheels. With it, the GLS450 managed a solid 5.1-second sprint to 60, eventually clearing the quarter-mile mark in an equally respectable 13.6 seconds at 101 mph. Not bad for a gas-powered machine that tipped our scales at 5623 pounds.

See all results for used cars for sale near 76010

Out in the real world, the powertrain only ever feels smooth. Whether we’re stomping on the right pedal or just breathing on it, the result is the same: a muted little growl and plenty of grunt. The transmission stays out of the spotlight; in fact, everything hiding under the body does its best to stay out of earshot. Our microphones picked up very little cabin noise, recording just 65 decibels (20 sones) at a 70-mph cruise. Insofar as high-end family transportation goes, the GLS450 nails that part of its assignment.

The GLS450’s cabin also succeeds in its goals—mostly. The materials are standard Mercedes-Benz fare, with plenty of nice-feeling leather and vinyl up top, while most of the harder materials remain low in the cabin, away from traditional touch points. Our test car had the no-charge six-seater option; the captain’s chairs in the second row are cushy and make third-row ingress and egress a breeze. The car’s so dang large that even adults can be reasonably comfortable all the way in back, with decent headroom and legroom that’s fine for short jaunts around town.

However, our editors didn’t fully embrace the cabin’s centerpiece: the Superscreen. This panoply of digital real estate spans the entire width of the dashboard, with a single piece of glass encasing the digital gauge cluster, the primary infotainment touchscreen, and the optional (and wholly superfluous) passenger screen. It’s basically eliminated the need to design a dashboard, which does a disservice to those who appreciate an aesthetic other than Blade Runner Dystopia. In fact, this pixel addiction is a growing problem across the entire Mercedes lineup. But hey, at least the steering wheel picked up a physical rocker and a thumbwheel.

See all results for used cars for sale near 76010

When it comes to the external half of the GLS-class’s refresh, the whole look gels, but like the revised S-class sedan before it, we’re wondering if Mercedes is going too hard in the paint on the self-branding. In addition to the gigantic three-pointed star on the grille, the grille itself now contains dozens of little three-pointed stars. Each headlight now has two three-pointed stars acting as running lights. In total, the rear lights contain six three-pointed stars. It’s a great design if you’re constantly forgetting what car you bought. Who are they trying to sell this thing to, the protagonist from Memento?

The GLS450’s more prominent bugbear is its ride quality. Ordinarily, a plush ride means road inconsistencies disappear, replaced with a body that floats serenely over juts and ruts without transmitting undue movement to the cabin and its occupants. In the GLS450, though, it appears the suspension engineers were tasked with reinventing body-on-frame jiggle from first principles. On any road that isn’t obsidian smooth, the GLS suffers from an awful lot of lateral wobbling after tackling a bump, and the body barely settles down by the time the next one arrives. It’s as if the engineers benchmarked an unladen F-350. Our test car was riding on the stock air suspension, and while it’s possible that upgrading to the electrohydraulic E-Active Body Control system would eliminate these unwanted movements, we’re let down that this setup ever left the plant in Alabama.

Despite a terminal case of the Wibbly-Wobblies, GLS450 proved surprisingly sticky around our 300-foot skidpad. We managed 0.92 g of lateral grip from the Pirelli P Zero PZ5 summer tires (285/40R-23 front, 325/35R-23 rear). The GLS also stopped from 70 mph in a tidy 154 feet. We’d appreciate these stats more if they didn’t come attached to a four-wheeled waterbed.

As if it wasn’t obvious from its segment positioning, the Mercedes GLS is an expensive proposition. It starts at $95,500, and you do get a good amount of standard equipment, including heated and ventilated front seats, air springs, all-wheel drive, and the Superscreen. Our test car picked up several add-ons—including $1620 for real leather and $3300 for the AMG Line design package—ballooning the price to $113,670. There’s a lot to like about the refreshed 2027 GLS450; we just wish ride quality was on that list.

#4480. Ford Mustang Dark Horse Driver Leads Police on Wild Chase Through Los Angeles Before Crash

The driver couldn't outrun the cops—but his passenger, apparently fresh out of jail for felony evading, insisted he could have.

Los Angeles County’s fabled Mulholland Drive is the perfect place to enjoy a Ford Mustang Dark Horse. Packed with tight curves, dramatic views, and homes owned by the rich and famous, the scenic route is one of the most famous roads in America. However, one Ford Mustang driver and his boastful passenger allegedly decided to turn it into a setting for a high-speed police chase.

According to reports by Fox 11 Los Angeles and The California Post, the pursuit began shortly after 1 a.m. on Thursday, November 5. Police reportedly had reason to believe that the Mustang was stolen, although authorities later specified that it was not. But their attempt to pull it over kicked off a chase that lasted nearly a half hour, with the Ford reportedly hitting speeds of about 80 miles per hour.

The driver reportedly didn’t stick to Mulholland Drive; he also jumped on Highway 101 and then Interstate 405, before eventually losing control and crashing on Woodcliff Road in Sherman Oaks. Authorities say that despite being injured, the driver tried to flee on foot after the crash but was quickly caught. The passenger was also detained, and he had some words for the police. “I just got out of the joint for felony evading,” the passenger told authorities, as captured on video. “If I was driving, you wouldn’t have caught me, I swear to God.”

In any event, the passenger was released after police questioned him. As for his buddy behind the wheel? He’s now facing felony evading charges of his own. A 500-horsepower Mustang Dark Horse may be made to eat up corners, but if those corners are on Mulholland Drive in the middle of the night—with police officers behind, no less—it might be better to keep those horses in the stable.

#4479. EVgo opens its first Tesla Superchargers, with hundreds more planned

EVgo has opened its first Supercharger station, and it’s in a Chicago grocery store parking lot. The site has 12 fast-charging stalls with both NACS and CCS plugs, and it’s the first of hundreds of Tesla Supercharger stalls EVgo plans to add across the US.

The 325 kW “EVgo Superchargers” are at Riverside Square & River’s Edge, at 3145 S Ashland Avenue. EVgo’s August announcement cited up to 500 kW for the Supercharger rollout.

The Chicago location features Magic Dock technology, which means both NACS and CCS vehicles can charge without an adapter. Drivers of compatible non-Tesla EVs can start a session through the Tesla app. If you drive a Tesla, the charging station shows up in the car’s navigation and Trip Planner. Other EVgo fast chargers with NACS plugs have been showing up in Tesla navigation since early September if you turn on third-party charging.

“By serving both Tesla and non-Tesla NACS drivers, we’re doubling EVgo’s addressable market and continuing to meet EV drivers where they are and where they want to charge,” said Badar Khan, EVgo CEO.

EVgo owns the Superchargers and self-brands them, and Tesla runs and maintains them. The first sites will be at Regency Centers shopping plazas with grocery stores.

Smart move on EVGo's part. More reliable charger at a lower cost than they can build themselves, and Tesla takes on all the maintenance and network operations for a slice of the sales.

EVgo is also adding NACS plugs to its regular fast-charging network, a rollout it started in 2025. The company aims to have 500 of those stalls across the US by the end of 2026, with Supercharger stalls counted separately. Over the next two years, it plans to put at least one NACS plug at every EVgo site built in 2023 or later.

#4478. Tesla's Kickflipping Roadster Looks Like A Great Way To Lose Your Lunch

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Car companies have spent the last 140 years figuring out how to perfect ground travel. Tesla decided that winning that war was unimaginative at best. And as we've all seen by now, the carmaker instead took its next-gen Roadster to the sky last month to demonstrate what it might look like to own a flying car one day.

But what would it actually be like to drive (fly?) the thing? This week, Tesla released a video showing a first-person camera view of the Roadster executing its rad kick-flip maneuver and other stunts. It does not look pleasant to experience firsthand.

If you watched the Roadster unveiling last month, this all probably looks familiar. It's the same stunts we saw that day, including the upside-down dive off of the half-pipe and the jump-spin over the Tesla Semi. But seeing it from the car's perspective adds a whole new layer to it, and shows this dizzying experience a person would have from the cockpit.

Watching the cold gas thrusters at work up close during the kickflip gives you a sense of how much goes into ensuring that the car stays upright. The car adjusts the volume of nitrogen that it releases in order to prevent car from over-rotating and transferring from a barrel roll to an out-of-control corkscrew. Just one simple nudge and it lands back on all four wheels.

Then there's the nosedive off of the half-pipe. A bit more correcting to keep the roll and yaw in check—but the Roadster does it without a hiccup.

All of these amazing stunts happened without a driver; Tesla put a dummy in the front seat. Many actual human beings might feel dizzy or even sick from these kinds of tricks.

Tesla hasn't published what kind of g-forces the kickflip generates, but watching the onboard footage also makes me wonder what kind of fighter pilot-style harness and big bolsters are needed to keep the driver in-place versus the road-going version of the car. Heck, you might need to be a fighter pilot to endure these maneuvers.

It's really hard not to appreciate how much engineering went into making the demo happen. Sure, it takes hours to fill up the 600-liter ultra-high-pressure composite-overwrapped pressure vessels with 10,000 PSI of nitrogen for just a few seconds of joy. But man, is it cool to watch from just about any perspective.

And while Tesla can't guarantee that the flying version of its car will reach a single driveway (or be road legal, for that matter), it's still a very cool, very over-engineered party trick unlike anything we'll likely see from a car manufacturer again. If you're going to buy one and put it through its paces, though, I'd recommend having a light lunch.

#4477. Yangwang U9 Xtreme Breaks Its Own Top Speed Record With 312.7-MPH One-Way Run

It’s the first production vehicle to surpass 500 kilometers per hour.

China’s Yangwang U9 Xtreme hypercar already held the record for fastest production car, but it seems the company wasn’t satisfied with that. The U9 Xtreme just beat itself—and crossed the 500 kilometer-per-hour barrier doing it.

With German racing driver Marc Bessing behind the wheel (the same man who piloted the car for its previous records), the U9 Xtreme hit 503.2 km/h during a run in Abu Dhabi on November 1. That’s 312.7 miles per hour. Unlike the previous record of 496.2 km/h (308.3 mph) that was set at Germany’s Papenberg track, this time, Yangwang took its electric hypercar to a closed public road; about six miles of Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed International Road was closed for the record run.

“Unlike a dedicated test track, a public road presents a different set of challenges, making precision, stability and confidence in the vehicle more important than ever,” Besseng said. “Breaking a world record once is extraordinary but doing it again in such a different environment is truly special.”

The road itself required sweeping prior to each run, and Yangwang spent two days running on the road before setting the record on the final pass. The company says it inspected every meter of the path for potential debris, even picking up rogue wire particles that could’ve been deposited from the cleaning brushes sweeping up.

Both the FIA and Guinness World Records have recognized the record as the highest speed achieved by a production car in a single-direction run. Updates to the car are credited for breaking the 500 km/h barrier versus last year’s 496.2 km/h run: Yangwang says it adjusted the angle of the rear wing to increase rear downforce, tweaked the suspension software to increase rebound damping “in response to subtle undulations in parts of the road,” and, changed tire pressure to increase high-speed stability.

In case you were wondering, the U9 Xtreme is fitted with four electric motors producing more than 2958 horsepower. It uses a 1200-volt battery pack, which is an upgrade over the regular U9’s 800-volt pack. As for the tire, Yangwang says it uses a specially designed tire from Giti Tire. Yangwang itself is a subsidiary of BYD, China’s largest automaker.

The next closest car to the U9 Xtreme is the Bugatti Chiron Super Sport that hit 304.8 mph back in 2019. In other words, Yangwang didn’t need to set this latest record to take back the crown. It simply ran the car for the love of the game, and of course to break that 500 km/h barrier.

The video is a fascinating watch, as Bessing spends plenty of time warming the tires and brakes before going for the run. He keeps it at about half or a little over half throttle until he gets past 380 km/h. From there on out, it’s full throttle as the car flies up to 480 km/h and creeps the rest of the way up to—and beyond—500 km/h.

#4476. Lincoln Is Bringing Back the Plug-In Hybrid Aviator in China

Lincoln is launching a new plug-in hybrid Aviator SUV in China, but we don’t expect to ever see it sold stateside.

Lincoln used to sell the Aviator SUV with an optional plug-in hybrid powertrain, but it was dropped from the lineup after 2023. Now, there’s a new Aviator PHEV in town, only this time, the towns it will be driving in will exclusively be across the Pacific Ocean. This is the Lincoln Aviator EX8, designed specifically for China and revealed via a regulatory filing with China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT).

Developed as part of Ford’s joint venture with Chinese automaker Changan, the new Aviator EX8 looks completely different from the Aviator SUV sold on our shores. It’s handsome and confident, with a blockier shape and an upright front end, and the large rectangular grille is adorned with a series of cascading chrome trim pieces. A large U-shaped trim piece spans the base of the front fascia, giving the SUV a planted look. It’s about the same size as the Aviator sold here, coming in a tad shorter, about an inch narrower, and roughly an inch taller. The rear is simple, with just a full-width rectangular taillight.

The EX8 is motivated by a plug-in hybrid powertrain. #4475. Hyundai’s $359 IONIQ 5 lease looks like a deal, but don’t overlook its bigger sibling

The Hyundai IONIQ 5 is the most popular EV in America outside of Tesla, but its larger three-row sibling looks like the better deal right now.

Through September, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 was the third top-selling EV in the US, behind the Tesla Model Y and Model 3.

Hyundai’s electric SUV is outselling rivals like the Chevy Equinox EV, Ford Mustang Mach-E, and Toyota bZ.

Why? For one, it’s one of the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at about $35,000, and Hyundai has been offering some of the most attractive lease deals.

After the $7,500 federal EV tax credit expired at the end of September last year, Hyundai responded by reducing prices on the IONIQ 5 by up to nearly $10,000 on some trims.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250. That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. Upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model adds $2,500, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Hyundai’s three-row electric SUV, the IONIQ 9, starts at $58,955, or nearly $24,000 more than the base IONIQ 5 SE.

On Hyundai’s website, the 2027 IONIQ 5 SE Standard Range is available to lease from $359 a month. The offer is for a 24-month lease with $4,999 due at signing for an effective cost of $567 per month.

The extended-range Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE RWD can be leased from $369 a month. The offer is also a 24-month lease with $4,999 due at signing, for an effective cost of $577 per month.

Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9, meanwhile, is available to lease from $419 a month. That deal also includes $4,999 due at signing, but is for a 36-month lease, so the effective cost is $557 per month.

Using Hyundai’s payment calculator, it would cost about $412 a month to lease the 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE for 36 months with $4,999 due at signing. With an effective cost of $550 per month, it’s only $7 less than the three-row IONIQ 9.

The Hyundai IONIQ 9 offers more range than its smaller sibling, with an EPA-estimated range of up to 335 miles for the base SE trim.

The IONIQ 5 is a midsize electric SUV, about the same size as a Tesla Model Y, with two rows and enough room for five passengers. Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9 offers three rows of seating and six- or seven-seat configurations.

With an added row of seating, the IONIQ 9 offers up to 163.54 cubic feet of interior passenger volume, compared with the IONIQ 5, which offers up to 106.5 cubic feet.

While the IONIQ 9 may be the better deal right now, the IONIQ 5 is still a good fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that doesn’t necessarily need the added space.

In comparison, the standard Tesla Model Y RWD is listed for lease starting at $499 a month with an EPA range of up to 321 miles. That’s for a 36-month lease with $3,000 down.

Using Tesla’s payment calculator, if you put the same $4,999 down for a 24-month lease like the IONIQ 5, the Model Y RWD’s monthly rate is $549.

Which one would you choose? The IONIQ 5, IONIQ 9, or Tesla Model Y? Let us know why in the comments.

Both the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are built at Hyundai’s Metaplant America outside of Savannah, Georgia.

I really haven’t seen much value in leasing. I’d rather buy the car outright using cash, with the goal of keeping the car for 10+ years.

My family recently bought a Hyundai IONIQ 5, and it is an outstanding car. Loaded with great features — both on the EV side and then for safety and comfort.

When we toured the facility earlier this year, Hyundai told us that its electric SUVs are attracting new buyers to the brand at a higher rate than its gas or hybrid vehicles.

The IONIQ 5 had a 69.8% conquest rate last year, while the IONIQ 9 had 64.3%. Hyundai’s Elantra N ranked third (61.9%), followed by the Palisade (61.2%) and Kona Electric (60.9%).

#4474. Tesla Is Now Powering One Of Its Biggest Charging Rivals

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Superchargers aren't just a Tesla thing anymore. Today EVgo announced that it opened its first location powered by Tesla hardware. The 12-stall charging station in Chicago kicks off an expansion that will include hundreds more Supercharger stalls nationwide, EVgo said.

With the shift to the North American Charging Standard (NACS), Tesla has shifted in some aspects toward a brand-agnostic tech provider. The NACS port was once a Tesla exclusive; now it’s the port of choice when it comes to modern EVs. Similarly, Tesla’s V4 Supercharging cabinets are available for purchase and installation by any commercial client. Tesla's V4 Supercharging cabinets are powerful, offering speeds up to 500 kW.

“Deploying our first EVgo Supercharger marks an important milestone in growing our customer base while supporting the EV industry’s transition to NACS,” said EVgo CEO Badar Khan.

The first EVgo location in Chicago has both CCS and NACS ports, thanks to the Magic Dock connector. The first batch of Tesla-powered EVgo stations will be built at grocery stores and shopping outlet centers owned by real estate company Regency Centers. This developer has had a longstanding partnership with EVgo; it already had plans to implement 400 more charging stalls. It says that Illinois is a great place to start its Supercharger push, since EV registrations have grown 60% over the past two years.

One nice bonus for Tesla drivers: EVgo’s Superchargers come up in Tesla’s in-car navigation system. As long as the “third-party charging” box is checked in the Tesla navigation app, users will be able to navigate to and charge just as easily as they would for a normal Tesla Supercharging station.

EVgo’s expansion spans more than just one developer or a handful of NACS ports. The company says it already is on track to hit 500 NACS-enabled charging stations nationwide (not counting the Supercharging network). Within the next two years, it wants all of its existing stations built after 2023 to have at least one NACS plug.

Tesla isn’t the only DC fast-charging company with hardware capable of charging natively via a NACS port. Once the NACS plug shape was officially certified by SAE, charging cabinet manufacturers quickly integrated it into their designs. However, Tesla’s Supercharging cabinets are known for their reliability. Tesla itself claims that uptime is 99%, and the network is known for being one of the best in the business.

In a recent survey of EV drivers, EVgo came in second place in terms of reliability after Tesla. Implementing more Tesla Supercharging cabinets could continue to elevate EVgo's reputation.

The German automaker just announced its $4 billion plans for its first U.S. plant, but it may already be considering a second phase of construction.

Audi hasn’t even broken ground on its newly announced $4 billion plans for a 1500-acre factory in Macon, Georgia, but the German automaker is already hinted at an additional $3 billion investment in the facility.

A new report from Reuters claims that Audi is already considering a second phase of construction at the Georgia plant. After pledging to invest an initial $4 billion, documents released by the Mid-Georgia Gateway Development Authority reportedly state that Audi will invest $3 billion more by 2033. Audi supposedly aims to employ an additional 3000 workers as part of the expansion plan.

The Trump Administration allegedly promised Audi some degree of tariff relief as part of the decision to build its first U.S. production facility; Reuters reported that Audi pushed for the European Union import duty to be lowered to 7.5 percent, but that the U.S. Commerce Department was expected to agree to around 10 percent. Currently, Audi imports all of its models to the U.S. from Europe and Mexico, and models from the EU are subject to a 15 percent tariff. Audi paid $1.4 billion in duties to the U.S. government last year.

Georgia is heavily incentivizing Audi’s decision to build in the Peach State: it is giving Audi the land, as well as providing $458 million in tax incentives and offering $120 million in grants. These grants will focus on infrastructure, rail improvements, environmental site remediation, and construction, according to Automotive News. The company will also be provided an additional $430 million in subsidies for water, road improvements, utility issues, workforce training, and recruitment.

Audi plans to produce its Q7, Q8, and Q9 SUVs at its future U.S. facilities. #4471. Apollo’s newest electric scooter is also its lowest-cost yet

Apollo has spent the last several years carving out a spot for itself toward the more premium end of the electric scooter market. Now the company is trying something different: going after the mass market with its least expensive model yet.

The new Apollo Dash carries a $699 MSRP, but is launching at $599 as part of the company’s Black Friday sale running through November 30. More importantly, Apollo says the Dash isn’t intended to simply be a stripped-down budget scooter, but rather a way to bring much of its existing technology down to a lower price point.

The scooter uses a 48V electrical system powering a 600W nominal, 1,200W peak-rated Bosch motor, with a top speed of 20 mph (32 km/h). Its 480Wh battery is rated for up to 25 miles (40 km) of range in Eco mode.

Apollo also claims the 48V architecture avoids limiting motor power to anemic levels as the battery drains, meaning riders shouldn’t experience the same increasingly sluggish performance toward the bottom of the battery that can occur on some lower-cost scooters.

At 43 lb (19.5 kg), the Dash is reasonably portable, though getting the weight and price down comes with an important compromise: there’s no suspension. Apollo also caps rider weight at 220 lb (100 kg), and points heavier riders or those regularly tackling rough roads and hills toward the more expensive Apollo Go instead.

Despite the lower price, there’s still a surprisingly long feature list. The Dash gets IP66 water resistance, self-healing tubeless tires, regenerative braking, built-in turn signals, Apollo’s Beam stem light, NFC unlocking, Apple Find My integration, and connectivity with the Apollo smartphone app.

Apollo says it put the frame through 10,000 km (6,200 miles) of durability validation before shipping production units. A beta test program also accumulated 1,002 miles over 144 rides without any reported punctures or maintenance issues. Beta riders averaged 19 miles (30 km) per ride while finishing with 29% battery remaining, according to Apollo.

Perhaps the bigger story here, though, is where Apollo is positioning the Dash. The company says 52% of its customers previously owned scooters from brands including Segway, NIU, and Xiaomi, but historically moving up to an Apollo often meant crossing the $1,000 mark.

At $599, the Dash appears designed to get those riders into Apollo’s ecosystem much earlier – while also putting the company squarely into competition with the mass-market scooters it previously sat above.

And for those wanting a bit more power or features, Apollo’s more upmarket models are on sale now as part of early Black Friday promotions.

BMW's latest Neue Klasse EVs push the boundaries of range and charging speed. In short, they're some damn good electric cars. Now there's another reason to buy one: free charging.

BMW on Thursday said it's offering $500 in public charging credits for 2027 electric models. It applies to the i5, i7, and iX3, and is open to drivers who buy or lease. The benefits last for one year from the car's purchase date.

Here's how the $500 breaks down. BMW says $300 of it can be redeemed at more than 15 charging networks, including Ionna, Shell Recharge, ChargePoint, and EVgo. The other $200 only applies to Ionna locations. (BMW is one of the automakers backing Ionna.)

To access the funds, drivers need to set up an account through the BMW app. Once they do that and handle payment through BMW ChargingNetwork, credits are automatically applied to eligible charging purchases.

BMW is also offering buyers of 2027 EVs one free year of Ionna membership, which gets drivers 25% discounts on sessions at the fast-growing charging player.

If $500 in free charging sounds nice and you're considering these vehicles, I have one note of caution after getting behind the wheel of all three.

The i5 is a solid all-around EV. It drives well, looks familiar, and offers over 300 miles of range in some trims. But the i7 and iX3 are miles ahead in terms of onboard technology and specs. The latter models use BMW's Neue Klasse architecture and feature an overhauled digital interface with a wonderful "Panoramic Vision" display below the windshield. The iX3 offers over 400 miles of range and 400 kilowatt charging. Expect similar capabilities to trickle throughout BMW's lineup and into the next iteration of the i5 too.

The 2027 RAV4 Woodland gets a new suspension system that gives it an additional inch of ground clearance.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 arrives with a collection of small tweaks that should add up to real improvements. Unfortunately, though not surprisingly, the new model year also comes with a slight price bump.

The 2027 RAV4 starts at $33,895 in front-drive LE trim, $36,695 for the front-drive SE, and $38,095 for the front-drive XLE Premium. Adding all-wheel drive to any of those trims incurs an additional $1600 cost. The AWD-only Woodland trim is up to $42,250, while the XSE is up to $43,495, and the Limited is up to $45,495. See all results for new 2027 Toyota RAV4 for sale near 20147

Every RAV4 thankfully now comes with a backup camera washer, and every AWD RAV4 gets Toyota’s Multi-Terrain Select modes. Plus, the Remote Connect trial is increasing from one year to five years, no matter the trim.

The bigger changes come when you zoom in. Woodland versions get redesigned all-weather floor and cargo mats. They also come with new suspension components, including springs, shocks, and jounce bumpers, that give them an additional inch of ground clearance. The granola-munching RAV4 now has 9.1 inches of clearance, compared with 8.1 inches for the rest of the lineup (aside from the GR Sport).

The first of the standard hybrid models will start arriving later this year, with plug-in models scheduled to launch in early 2027.

#4468. The Iambic Model T Is the Luxury Sneaker Built for Life at the Racetrack

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Italian leather, custom comfort, and auto-inspired design make these my favorite shoes for Formula 1 weekends.

There’s something fitting about the Model T sneaker becoming my favorite for race weekends. Much like the cars we obsess over, the Iambic Model T takes an engineering-first approach to comfort, combining modern technology, thoughtful construction, and premium materials.

Think of it like commissioning a luxury grand tourer. A Ferrari isn’t simply about horsepower; it’s about the materials, the craftsmanship, and attention to the person behind the wheel. Iambic applies the same philosophy, from its Italian leather to its personalized fit.

After wearing mine throughout the year, across Europe and the U.S., I'm convinced the approach works.

Rather than relying on conventional shoe sizing, Iambic uses AI-assisted technology to create a personalized fit. The process begins with a smartphone app that captures images of your feet and collects information about your comfort preferences. It may seem unusual, but I promise it makes sense. Through the app, you will send pictures of each foot from different angles to capture the full scope and how you stand. That data helps determine how your shoes are made. These foot scans showed me that I wear slightly more on my right side because of an old skating injury, something I never knew.

The Model T is handcrafted in Portugal using Italian full-grain leather, with a triple-layer rubber sole, adjustable foam insoles, and a padded heel collar. It’s an impressive combination.

For someone accustomed to appreciating the details inside a well-appointed Italian automobile, that approach feels familiar. The materials matter, but so does how everything works together.

I’ve worn my white Model Ts all over Modena’s cobblestone streets with my family, through multiple days at racetracks, and across America on my 36-hour Route 66 road trip. They’ve become my favorite driving and racing shoes, and that says a lot.

Anyone who’s attended a race knows how much walking it involves. Between navigating sprawling circuits, standing for hours, and sometimes carrying equipment or bags, your footwear gets a serious workout.

Silverstone was the ultimate test. Four consecutive days of traversing the circuit left my sneakers considerably dirty, but my feet stayed unswollen and blister-free. I didn’t even wear socks with them the last day (so they wouldn’t clash with my Fernando outfit). They were so comfortable that I rarely thought about my feet, even when walking across the hilly, uneven grounds and up and down the grandstand.

They also became my preferred driving shoes for long-haul trips with my cousin. Their fit and manageable sole made hours and hours in the driver’s seat enjoyable, without the bulk of traditional athletic sneakers. And despite the punishment they underwent, a basic leather-cleaning kit brought the white back to life.

At $600, the Model T belongs in the same conversation as other premium footwear, but the appeal goes beyond appearance. You’re investing in personalized construction, a sneaker designed for serious use and only for you. After a full season of travel, mine have more than justified their price.

With Austin, Texas, behind us and Las Vegas approaching, remember that a Grand Prix involves considerably more walking than most first-time attendees anticipate. Every year, social media fills with photos of blistered feet from fans who chose fashionable boots or sleek loafers over comfort. My advice? Save the fancy boots and dress shoes for dinner.

If you’re already investing in the experience of attending a Formula 1 race, or any race, the right footwear makes perfect sense. Like a beautifully engineered Italian sports car, the Iambic Model T proves performance and luxury can coexist.

#4467. Gas Prices Got You Down? This 261-MPG Volkswagen Solves That—For $140,000

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

In 2013, VW launched one of the most fascinating experiments in fuel efficiency ever made. The Volkswagen XL1 took 12 years to develop and ended up costing a whopping $150,000 at the time. However, as an engineering exercise, it was brilliant. And since VW only made 250, it's even rarer than a Bugatti Veyron from the same era.

If you're looking for an extreme answer to high gas prices, today's your lucky day. There's currently an XL1 in the Netherlands up for auction on Catawiki. The 2016 model up for grabs has just over 1,000 miles on the odometer and is apparently in excellent condition inside and out.

The XL1 project was spearheaded by Ferdinand Piech, VW's top boss at the time. Not known to ever give up on his lofty, ambitious goals, Piech fought for 12 years, and through several iterations, to finally achieve his "one liter" car, something that could burn just one liter of fuel per every 100 km. VW pulled out all the stops to make it extraordinarily efficient; the result was something closer to a supercar than a Toyota Prius.

That teardrop-shaped body is made from carbon fiber, as is its chassis, saving weight. It debuted a full year before BMW's i3, an EV/PHEV which only had a carbon chassis but a plastic body. The car has butterfly doors and two seats that are offset to optimize the car's aerodynamic shape.

Power comes from an 800cc, two-cylinder, turbo-diesel engine behind the driver—this makes it mid-engine, like a supercar—plus a plug-in hybrid system centered around a 5.5 kilowatt-hour battery. The plug-in hybrid powertrain wasn't originally planned, and didn't come about until near the end of its development, so it needed a massive 50-pound removable charging box in the trunk so you could plug it in.

With a funky hybrid powertrain, a curb weight of just 1,852 pounds, and a drag coefficient of just 0.189, the XL1 was capable of an EU-tested 0.9 liters per 100 km, which equates to 261 mpg. It can also travel 31 miles on battery power alone, registering an insane efficiency of 6.2 miles per kWh, about double today's more conventional EVs. VW said at the time of the XL1's launch that it only needed about 8 horsepower to sustain a steady 62 mph.

The main downside is performance: It only makes 68 horsepower, so it takes almost 13 seconds to get to 60 mph.

This specific car up for auction is expected to fetch around $140,000, according to the auction house. So even with its incredible fuel economy and currently outrageous fuel prices, the XL1's financial breakeven point is still a long ways away. Plus, it runs on diesel, which has seen even steeper price spikes than regular gas. A used EV cuts you off from the gas station entirely, and is a better all-around choice of course.

But for someone who wants an amazing piece of automotive history, the XL1 could be worth the price. Plus, it'll sip on fuel like no other for many of your daily errands—and look cool doing it.

#4466. Amazon set to deploy more than 3,000 TATA electric delivery trucks

Amazon isn’t just electrifying its American delivery operations. The virtual big box stores that Bezos built understands the benefits of EVs as well as anyone, and they’re working hard to deploy electric vehicles everywhere they can. And now, that global push is extending to India.

Indian automaker TATA Motors has announced a deal with Amazon to deploy 3,000 electric trucks across Amazon’s transportation network in India. When it goes live, it will be the largest electric truck deployment by in India and mark Amazon’s most significant move to extend its Indian fleet electrification beyond last-mile logistics.

“India is accelerating towards electric mobility and the realization of Viksit Bharat 2047,” says Shri H.D. Kumaraswamy, Hon’ble Union Minister for Heavy Industries and Steel, Government of India. “The collaboration between TATA Motors and Amazon shows what that looks like in practice: sustained demand from a nationwide logistics network met by electric trucks manufactured in India. Through PM E-DRIVE, the Government will continue to support this transition, and I look forward to more such efforts in powering green logistics.”

In addition to being a big deal for TATA, the 3,000 electric truck deal represents a serous bump to India’s deployed electric truck fleet, and are a major step towards the wide-scale electrification of freight transportation across the country – that’s not just good for Amazon’s fuel bills, it’s good for everyone and everything that breathes air, too.

“Electrifying our logistics and transportation network is an important part of Amazon’s goal to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2040,” says Abhinav Singh, Vice President, Operations, Amazon, APAC, Middle East, Africa and Turkey. “We have made significant progress in India, with more than 15,000 electric vehicles operating across 500-plus cities. To enable this transition, we are also supporting the development of infrastructure and solutions that make EV adoption easier for our carrier partners and drivers. We are now setting a bold vision to scale electric trucking, addressing one of the toughest challenges in decarbonizing transportation. Our collaboration with TATA Motors marks an important step towards realizing this vision. By combining our strengths, we aim to accelerate the deployment of electric trucks across more routes, starting with intracity operations and expanding to India’s major freight corridors.”

The truck Amazon will be deploying in these record numbers is a version of the Tata Ultra E.7, a 7.5-tonne (~16,000 lb.) straight truck powered by a 240 kW (~320 hp) electric motor drawing power from a 96 kWh LFP battery pack. The truck’s makers claim a loaded range of up to 130 km (~80 miles) on a single charge, with DC fast-charging that’s capable enough to keep the trucks charged up between deliveries.

Amazon’s new TATA electric delivery trucks will support the transport of goods between warehouse facilities – which means traveling across cities and along India’s national freight corridors.

#4465. Every Brand Selling Sports Cars in the U.S. in 2027

From Aston Martin to Toyota, this is every performance two-door car for sale in the United States.

Whether you love cars or merely tolerate them as basic transportation, we can all admit that sports cars are cool. The best sports cars stimulate the senses, whether it’s the sound of a powerful engine or the scent of expensive leather. Sports cars make our lives better, and you'll be doing the world a service by buying one.

That's why we've gathered all the new sports cars on sale for 2027. Only two-door vehicles engineered and marketed by their manufacturers strictly for performance (and fun) are included in this list. We have lists for sporty sedans and SUVs, but not here. If you want the pinnacle of excitement from the world's most renowned car brands, read on.

The grandest of all grand tourers come from Aston Martin. The DB12 and Vanquish aim for elegance with their clean, timeless designs, while the smaller Vantage is gorgeous all to itself. For a 1064-hp hypercar with polished road manners, consider a Valhalla.

Bentley's brutish approach to sports cars is the same in 2027 as it was in 1927. The Continental GT is a heavyweight that can handle, as evidenced by the latest Supersports model. The plug-in hybrid models offer greater comfort, with up to 771 hp.

Since the Z4 roadster departed, BMW is without a true two-seat sports car. What's left are two hard-core M cars with small back seats: the M2 coupe and the M4 coupe and convertible. If you dislike BMW's latest Neue Klasse designs, these cars are Alt Klasse in the best ways.

While the Camaro is on hiatus yet again, Chevy has four enticing Corvette variants ranging from supercar contender to million-dollar winner. They all undercut their European rivals on price, too. A new 6.7-liter V-8 is in for 2027, and it improves the performance of the lower-end Stingray and Grand Sport models considerably. America's sports car is at its absolute peak.

Although most mere mortals won’t ever be able to purchase one, the Ferrari hype is real. The company's expertise in electronic chassis control, plus the sheer brilliance of its six-, eight, and 12-cylinder engines, are the gold standards of the sports-car world. Ferrari deserves every love letter it gets.

Since 1964, there's been a Mustang for everyone, though in 2027, everyone who wants a V-8 Mustang better have at least $50K. Affordability aside, the Mustang matters. It's a classic sports car with the sound, fury, and the hardware to compete with the world's best—and that includes the $328,000 GTD.

We're not including Honda's heavy hitter, the Civic Type R, since it's a hatchback. For pure sports cars, the Prelude fills in with a pretty exterior, but it's effectively a Civic Hybrid coupe that starts at $44K.

As the party animal of any sports car gathering, Lamborghini likes to play loud and could care less who it wakes up at 3 am. The Temerario revs to 10,000 rpm and kicks up tremendous amounts of debris from the exposed rear tires. The Revuelto SV has 1050 horsepower with doors that open skyward, as they should.

Lotus has gone through many ups and downs over the years, but it gets one car right. The mid-engined Emira sports car is an analog machine with a dialed-in chassis, sultry styling, and the distinctive character you'd expect of a hand-built British car.

Maserati's beautiful sports cars with their rich, decadent interiors and twin-turbo V-6 engines are often overlooked by wealthy buyers who would rather buy yet another black 911. For those with great taste and total confidence, the GranTurismo, GranCabrio, and the MCPura offer a distinctive alternative to the norm.

The fundamentals of an excellent sports car start with an MX-5 Miata. It’s small and remarkably lightweight, which puts Mazda in a class of one for building a two-seat, rear-wheel drive, manual transmission roadster that costs under $40K. It can also be had with a power targa roof in the RF (Retractable Fastback) model.

McLaren is re-doing its logo, but fear not: the cars are the same technical masterpieces that feel like sports cars of old. Whether it's the plug-in hybrid Artura, the roomy GTS, or the race-ready 750S, a McLaren delivers raw excitement with expert control.

AMG’s high-performance models are known for being hot, fast, loud, and desirable. The widebody CLE53 coupe and convertible, the iconic SL roadster, and the slick GT Coupe are the Benzes we really want.

Maybach glitzes up and quiets down the AMG SL for a plusher convertible with the coveted Mercedes hood ornament. But rest assured, an SL680 in Maybach form is ready to rip when asked.

An oldie and very much a goodie, the Z is a sports car legend with an illustrious history. The current model features classic lines and a manual transmissions, and you’re unlikely to see another one like it in the neighborhood. Sign us up.

The daddy of all sports cars, Porsche is the first and last name for engineering perfection. Without a 718 Boxster or Cayman for 2027, it's the 911's job to keep the brand's heritage in full swing across its dozens of variants. It's fantastic almost to a fault, as so many people buy them that they start seem ordinary.

As the only gas-powered rear-wheel-drive car in Subaru's lineup, the BRZ is an elemental sports car that, like a Mazda MX-5 Miata, is a great teacher of driving skill. It's basic, relatively cheap, and always fun.

Toyota was the mastermind behind the partnership that bore the original Scion FR-S and Subaru BRZ. With the latest GR86, Toyota's essence of simplified, driver-focused engineering is on full display, especially now that the Supra has departed.

#4464. Farah: Why a Fender Bender in My Porsche Taycan Cost $35,000

A minor accident in my late-model EV nearly totaled it, and the battery pack was partly to blame.

I love cars, but I also know cars are bad for the environment, whether they are powered by gas, electric, or diesel. New cars, in particular, take energy and raw materials to build, and often cost more to run and maintain. For me, that upfront environmental impact is all the more reason to keep older, efficient cars on the road even in the face of rising repair costs. But there must be a balance in the quest for efficiency.

If you do care about the planet, the most efficient choice in the U.S. right now is to buy a used, well-maintained EV. No one built a brand new car for you, and the carbon footprint from assembling it is now spread across multiple owners. The longer you drive it, the cleaner it is (versus a combustion car).

For nearly two years, I have been driving around L.A. in what was, as of December of 2024, the cheapest used Porsche Taycan Cross Turismo in the United States. I love EVs for driving around cities just as much as I love a high-compression, light-flywheel, manual gearbox, mid-engined monster for a canyon run: each is fit for its purpose. I did not buy a used EV to make some kind of political or environmental statement—I saw personal value and a fun public experiment. After all, a Taycan depreciates rapidly from new, and not because it’s a badly made car.

What originally stickered for $139,000 was mine for $64,800 plus tax with only 26,000 miles. Over the approximately 12,000 miles since, it has been a superb car: comfortable, fast, dynamic, and overwhelmingly reliable, albeit with a few software hiccups and two genuine mechanical repairs, all sorted under the Porsche Certified pre-owned unlimited-mile warranty. Although a Taycan is still a semi-exotic Porsche to many, the four-seat electric wagon is my family’s most “normal” car.

Which is why I let a friend borrow it for a trip to the lake with his wife. My friend isn’t a car enthusiast, but he had no history of accidents, shenanigans, or other red flags in the 30 years I’ve known him. The perfect person to trust with a loan. And so I never would have predicted the phone call I received over that weekend: He’d been in an accident with my car.

Fortunately, no one was hurt. Also fortunately (for our relationship), the accident wasn’t his fault, as insisted by him, bolstered by a police report, and cosigned by my insurance adjuster. In fact, he was stopped at a red light and rear-end/sideswiped by a young woman who, as it turns out, had a long history of accidents in her short driving career.

And while I was upset to get the phone call, my rage subsided quickly when I saw the accident site photo. This didn’t look like a big deal at all. The rear bumper was scraped, and perhaps the parking sensor was damaged. The painted-over fender needed replacing, as did the HRE 522M wheel. I figured maybe $3000-4000 for the body work, another $4000 for the wheel, a couple of weeks in the shop, and that would be that.

It would be 73 days, and it would cost my insurance company over $35,000 before I got my car back. Hypothetically, if the car was not insured under an agreed-value classic car collector’s policy, it would likely have been outright totaled, despite being easily repairable.

It turns out the impact on the damaged wheel, plus the force of the car being shoved several feet while the brakes were applied, damaged the air suspension. It wasn’t just damaged on the corner that was hit. Both the gas strut and control arm assembly were cracked on the opposite corner as well, even without a direct impact! When the air suspension lost pressure, the air supply unit, control module, and a bunch of other four-figure components went down with it. Once the suspension needs to be disassembled to that degree, Porsche isn’t going to reassemble it with old hardware, so the invoice includes thousands in bolts, bushings, collar nuts, washers, carriers, and so on.

And because it's an EV, performing this work requires removing the high-voltage battery pack: 24 hours at $340 an hour. If you aren’t used to paying for mechanical work, this is a huge rate, even for Porsches, even in Los Angeles.

So while the cosmetic bodywork amounted to little more than $5000 or $6000, the mechanical and electrical repairs escalated like Bitcoin in 2020, eventually landing in the mid-twenties. Factor in a new wheel from HRE, three flatbed transports, and assorted random billables, and that’s how the total made it to $35,000.

The air suspension took second place on the bill; the Achilles' heel for late-model luxury car service, gas or electric alike. It was almost $20,000. This and all other repairs would have been similar to a gas-powered Panamera or Cayenne. But if you're predisposed to hate EVs, here's another piece of ammunition towards that view. Nearly $8000 of this bill, over 20% of it, went to battery pack labor. (The pack itself was, and is, totally fine).

As these once-pricey EVs get cheaper, the cost of repairs raises the value required to avoid getting totaled. This is a shame. Otherwise working, good-condition cars with most of their carbon footprint already amortized might be scrapped. Yes, battery packs and cells can be recycled, but it’s not done at a large enough scale yet. More importantly, the best thing we can do for the environment is keep already-built EV’s on the road for as long as possible. Fortunately, battery packs are lasting longer in cars than originally expected (ironically part of the reason for the slow build of the battery recycling ecosystem).

To their credit, both South Bay Certified Collision Center in Torrance, CA, and McKenna Porsche did an excellent job repairing my car. This is not a story about getting ripped off, and I’m not arguing that any other shop could do it cheaper. The fact that my Taycan got a completely refreshed air suspension means it drives perhaps even better than it did before. And because I have agreed value insurance and the accident wasn’t my fault, none of the enormous stack of dollars it took to fix my car came out of my pocket. I could have chosen to total the car, but I chose to fix it. Such is the benefit of that type of policy. And I intend to keep driving this car because I very much like it.

If we are going to have more EV’s, which we should, because they are good for many things, then we need to ensure that these cars survive minor collisions. That could mean changing what the word “totaled” means for an EV on the insurance side. It could also mean training up enough technicians so that a battery pack removal doesn’t command a higher hourly rate than what I pay for Lamborghini Countach restoration. It should also mean that car companies, perhaps German ones, should design battery packs so that they’re more easily removed or that other major components can be replaced around them.

In either case, we can’t have EVs meeting a premature demise. There’s nothing more wasteful than a car that could be working, but without working math to justify fixing it.

#4463. Tesla Is Killing The Cybertruck To Make Room For More Robotaxis

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The controversial Tesla Cybertruck electric pickup will be retired next year, CEO Elon Musk confirmed on X. The angular truck went on sale at the end of 2023 and instantly became a social statement—for better or worse.

Production of the Cybertruck will start winding down next summer at the company’s Texas Gigafactory, and the extra floor space will be used to build more Cybercabs.

The unpainted truck had a short burst in popularity at the beginning of its production run, but interest fizzled, and sales never reached the potential that Musk and Tesla had envisioned back in 2019, when the vehicle was first presented as a concept.

In this year’s third quarter, the Cybertruck amassed 4,323 sales, according to data from Cox Automotive. From January through September, sales totaled 11,586 units. Tesla doesn’t break out individual sales figures for the Cybertruck, but industry estimates put the vehicle’s overall deliveries at roughly 70,000.

That’s a far cry from the hundreds of thousands of sales recorded every quarter by the Model 3 and Model Y. It’s also another reminder that electric pickups haven’t quite taken off as their manufacturers had hoped, and Tesla is now taking the fall, just like Ford did with the F-150 Lightning, which went the way of the dodo last year after lackluster sales and ballooning costs.

There’s no denying that you either love or hate the Cybertruck, just like there’s no denying that Tesla dared to do things like no other car manufacturer before it. Sure, some might argue that the angular EV looks like an unpolished fridge, but it brought steer-by-wire and a 48-volt low-voltage architecture to the masses. Whether or not they’ll be adopted by other companies is another story, though.

At roughly the same time as Elon Musk’s announcement that Cybertruck production would wind down in the middle of 2027, Tesla stopped taking orders for the entry-level Dual-Motor All-Wheel Drive version of the model, leaving just the Premium and Cyberbeast trims available to order on the automaker’s website.

Additionally, the price of the remaining models has been increased. The Premium AWD model now starts at $92,490, up from $89,990, while the top Cyberbeast now costs $102,490, up from $99,990. The most recent price bumps come after a similar move in August.

#4462. Honda just showed off its first high-end electric mountain bike

Honda makes just about everything with a motor, from lawnmowers and generators to cars, motorcycles, and even airplanes. Now the Japanese giant is adding another electrified vehicle to the list – a premium electric mountain bike.

Unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the new Honda RN0 marks the company’s first entry into the premium electric mountain bike market. And unlike many automotive-branded e-bikes that amount to little more than a licensing deal and a familiar logo slapped on someone else’s frame, Honda appears to have actually put some engineering muscle behind this one.

The RN0 was jointly developed with German high-end e-MTB manufacturer ROTWILD and features a proprietary carbon monocoque frame and distinctive gull-arm swingarm inspired by Honda’s motorcycle chassis development experience.

There’s actually some real history behind that connection. Honda experimented with mountain bike development in the early 2000s, culminating in its wild RN01 downhill racing bike. In 2005, that project won the overall series championship in the UCI Mountain Bike Downhill World Cup. Honda never turned the RN01 into a consumer bicycle, but more than two decades later, the RN0 is effectively picking up where the company previously left off.

The roughly 24 kg (53 lb) RN0 is set up as a multi-role electric mountain bike, featuring 160 mm FOX 36 FLOAT Factory Kashima front suspension paired with a FOX FLOAT X Factory Kashima rear shock. DT Swiss H1900 SPLINE wheels use a mullet setup with a 29-inch wheel up front and 27.5-inch wheel in the rear, while Shimano DEORE XT four-piston brakes handle stopping duties.

Those are some quality components, but the drivetrain may be even more interesting.

Honda is using Shimano’s new 2.3 kg drive unit, rated for up to 100 Nm of torque and 750 watts of maximum output, paired with a sizeable 720 Wh battery.

Shimano’s AUTO ASSIST can automatically vary motor assistance based on terrain and rider input, while AUTO SHIFT handles gear changes to maintain an appropriate cadence.

There’s even an Assist Carryover function that briefly continues providing power after pedaling stops, potentially making it easier to clear rocks, roots, and other technical obstacles that normally would see the assist grind to a halt right when it is needed most.

A 2.2-inch color display is integrated directly into the top tube, and there’s USB-C charging plus Shimano app connectivity for adjusting motor settings and electronically locking the bike.

Honda hasn’t yet announced pricing in its release, but with a carbon chassis, Factory-level FOX suspension, XT brakes, and premium Shimano electronics, don’t expect this to be the everyman’s electric bike.

If anything, the RN0 looks much more like Honda is finally bringing its motorcycle engineering mentality back to mountain bikes – this time with a battery and motor along for the ride.

#4461. 2027 Tesla Cybertruck

See all results for new 2027 Tesla Cybertruck for sale near ?

The Cybertruck’s styling gets a lot of attention, but under the skin is a capable and useful workhorse on par with other electric pickups. All models come with all-wheel drive, and a height-adjustable air-spring suspension system gives you more ground clearance for off-road adventures. A 593-hp dual-motor setup is standard; the Cyberbeast trim gets an 834-hp tri-motor powertrain.

Inside, you will find Tesla’s signature minimalist interior design, with a large center touchscreen on the dash housing virtually all of the truck’s gauges and controls. A yoke-style steering wheel and variable-ratio electric power steering take some getting used to, but once you’re up and running, you will find the Cybertruck to be easily maneuverable.

Expert Tip: The Cybertruck’s stainless-steel body comes unpainted. Plus, it attracts fingerprints just like your home’s stainless steel kitchen appliances. If that sounds like it might get on your nerves, you may want to consider the cost of a vehicle wrap in your buying decision.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk has announced that production of the Cybertruck will end mid-2027, so if you want one, you need to act quickly.

Compare the 2027 Tesla Cybertruck with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.

The base rear-wheel drive single-motor model from last year has been discontinued, leaving the dual-motor all-wheel drive variant to serve as the Cybertruck lineup’s entry-level model. Tesla CEO Elon Musk has announced that production of the Cybertruck will end mid-2027, so if you want one you ought to act quickly.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

The base and Premium trims feature the same 593-hp dual-motor powertrain. Those looking for mind-bending performance will want the Cyberbeast, which features a trio of motors making a combined 834 horses. The Premium and Cyberbeast trims have an adjustable air suspension that can raise or lower the EV on the fly to provide up to 16 inches of ground clearance; the base models make do with conventional coil-spring suspension with adaptive dampers.

All Cybertrucks boast impressive 35-degree approach and 28-degree departure angles, so the Tesla pickup should be a formidable off-road machine. On the road, the big Cybertruck feels more agile than expected. We drove a Cyberbeast and found its combination of rear-wheel steering and variable-ratio steer-by-wire tech made for easy maneuvering in urban environments.

In Comparison: The tri-motor Cyberbeast's 2.6-second 60-mph time makes it quicker than the quad-motor Rivian R1T, which needed 3.0 seconds to get to the same speed. Even more impressive, the Cyberbeast's 60-mph time matches that of the Chevy Corvette C8 Z06.

The Premium and Cyberbeast models have a maximum towing capacity of 11,000 pounds, while the base trim is rated to tug 7500 pounds. Payload varies by model and tire choice, but an all-terrain-shod Cybertruck Premium can haul the most, carrying 2500 pounds in its six-by-four-foot composite cargo bed.

The Tesla Cyberbeast's battery capacity is approximately 122.4 kWh. Tesla claims the base model can recoup 132 miles in 15 minutes when hooked up to a Supercharger. In the same timeframe, the Premium model can restore 137 miles while the Cyberbeast adds 135. In our testing, it took 50 minutes to charge the Cyberbeast's battery from 10 to 50 percent.

Since the Cybertruck is technically considered a heavy-duty pickup truck by the EPA's standards, Tesla isn't required to report fuel-economy figures to the government agency. We observed 55 MPGe in mixed driving with a Cyberbeast.

First Row: Those who thought the Tesla Model 3's interior was minimalistic will relive that reaction when they see the Cybertruck's spartan cabin. The base model boasts heated front seats and a single central touchscreen, while the other two have seat heating and ventilation, plus a second screen for rear-seat passengers.

Second Row: Headroom is surprisingly generous in the rear seat given the truck's dramatically sloped roofline, but riders over six feet tall may find it snug.

Cargo Capacity: In our testing, we found that the truck's front trunk (frunk) holds just one carry-on suitcase, but the interior will fit 22 with the rear seats folded. The Cybertruck's cargo bed offers 121 cubic feet of volume, and inside the bed is a hidden underfloor storage compartment that’s large enough to fit an additional suitcase.

Every Cybertruck has a big 18.5-inch touchscreen mounted in the center of the dashboard. In the Premium and Cyberbeast, there's also a 9.4-inch touchscreen on the back of the center console for rear-seat passengers. SiriusXM satellite radio is included, as is a Wi-Fi hotspot, but drivers hoping for Apple CarPlay and Android Auto will be disappointed, as those features do not appear in any Tesla model.

Every Cybertruck comes standard with Tesla's controversial Autopilot driving feature. The brand's Full Self-Driving (supervised) system is optional. Neither system yet enables fully autonomous driving, something Tesla has long promised. The company also provides other, more basic driver-assistance technology.

For information about the Cybertruck's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

Tesla provides a comprehensive warranty on its current models; however, it doesn't include any complimentary maintenance.

#4460. Teaser for Honda’s Future Japanese-Market Crossover May Hint at Designs for America

The 0-Series EV line may never reach production, but the new logo and design language those cars inspired seem to be on the way soon.

When Honda abandoned its plans to release a series of 0-Series-branded electric vehicles earlier this year, it also effectively abandoned the first cars that would have been released in the company’s bold new design language. That certainly does not mean the new look of Honda is being tabled forever, though. We already know from a hybrid sedan concept shown in May that the visual identity of the 0-Series EVs would live on—and now, we have our first look at a production car that shares that fresh look.

Both Honda of Australia and Honda of Japan posted a teaser for a model called the Avancier on Friday, revealing a first look at an SUV expected to be targeted primarily at those markets. Notably, the model appears to bear a passing resemblance to both the scrapped 0-Series SUV and the May concept. “Honda Hybrid” badging also suggests that the Avancier will be one of the company’s first cars to use the brand’s next-generation gas-electric powertrain.

The Avancier badge has previously been used on a turn-of-the-millennium station wagon for Japan, as well as a Chinese-built crossover offered in that market. This new model seems to be a crossover targeted at other markets, something that could be equivalent to the American CR-V or Passport. A representative from American Honda has confirmed to Road & Track that the Avancier itself is not coming to the U.S. market.

Details of the final model, including specifics of the Honda Hybrid powertrain, may prove irrelevant to American buyers, but the styling and the concepts behind the hybrid system could preview what to expect when Honda unveils a fast-tracked new CR-V for the United States in the near future.

#4459. Over A Quarter Of BMW, Mini, And Rolls-Royce Models Sold In Q3 Had A Plug

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The BMW Group, which operates the BMW, Mini, and Rolls-Royce car brands, saw 20% of its global vehicle sales in the third quarter represented by all-electric models. Adding plug-in hybrids increases the electrified models’ share to 27.4%, the company said in its latest earnings report.

From the beginning of the year through September, EVs have accounted for 18.4% of the three automakers’ total sales worldwide, with PHEVs raising the figure to 26.1%.

Despite the promising numbers, the automotive group clearly has a regionalization problem on its hands. Europe is leading the way by a wide margin, with 34.7% of sales represented by EVs and 46.9% by all electrified models.

Meanwhile, over in the United States, just 4.7% of BMW, Mini, and Rolls-Royce models sold were EVs. That’s a huge difference, and it puts the U.S. at the bottom of the BMW Group’s list for electrification. By comparison, Chinese EV sales amounted to 6.5%, while the Asia-Pacific, Eastern Europe, Middle East, and Africa regions totaled 18% EV sales.

The only thing that saves the day for the company’s electrified lineup in the U.S. is plug-in hybrids, which, together with EVs, had an 11.4% share in the third quarter. It’s also worth noting that the new iX3 and i3 models are just starting to trickle down to American dealers, and the U.S. also doesn’t get the electric iX2 and iX2 that Europeans have access to. The updated i7 is also on its way, but that has always been a low-volume car that never made a meaningful impact on the company’s sales reports.

What’s more, even though one in every five BMW Group models was all-electric in Q3, the company’s year-to-date numbers aren’t so promising. Globally, the group sold 314,552 EVs and 131,653 PHEVs from January through September, a 5.1% decrease compared to the same period last year. EVs saw a 2.7% drop, while PHEV sales declined 10.3%.

The only positive number in the company’s electrification Excel sheets has to do with how many EVs were sold in comparison to everything else in the portfolio. In the first three quarters of 2026, the share of EV sales within the BMW Group reached 18.4%, up from last year’s 18%.

Things should improve once the iX3 and i3 are widely available everywhere in the world, but they’re not guaranteed to be a success in the U.S., where policy whiplash has severely slowed the adoption of all-electric vehicles.

#4458. 5 American, 6 Canadian: Workhorse W56 arrives in the True North

Electric truck brand Workhorse is bringing its W56 Class 5 and 6 electric trucks to Canada thanks to a new agreement with a Canadian dealer group and fleet management provider offering truck and trailer sales, parts, repair, and 24/7 roadside assistance and towing services across the Northern nation.

Building on years of electric step van deployments in Canada and underscoring the company’s commitment to Canada as a growth region, the new dealer agreement with Tristan Fleet Management marks the first-ever Canadian dealer partnership for Workhorse.

“Canadian fleets need proven electric trucks that deliver on quality and performance in any condition,” said James Griffin, Chief Revenue Officer at Workhorse. “The W56 has already proven itself on this front in real-world fleet service across Canada. Tristan’s strong reputation, its extensive network, and ability to provide around-the-clock roadside support will be extremely valuable as Workhorse continues to grow our presence in the country.”

Workhorse has been selling and supporting electric trucks in Canada since 2021 through its partnership with Purolator, a Canadian-owned leading integrated freight, package and logistics solutions provider that has grown alongside the rapid expansion of online shopping for everything from groceries to car parts and road-ready motorcycles has also seen the expansion of last-mile delivery contractors. These fleet operators and drivers are essential workers who keep the online economy rolling, and they are getting positively pummeled by this year’s record fuel prices, a product of America’s latest “dumb oil war” in Iran.

And, after Workhorse’ fleet logged its 20 millionth mile driven with zero tailpipe emissions, you could hardly claim that it’s an unknown quantity – a fact that Tristan understands.

“Our customers have been exploring electrification for some time now,” explains Daniel Barbu, Tristan’s Vice President and General Manager. “With generous incentives from Écocamionnage, as well as the current extremely high cost of fuel, the business case for going electric has never been stronger … we’re looking forward to helping Workhorse expand its customer base across Canada and supporting our customers meet their own goals for sustainability and vehicle performance.”

Tristan operates out of seven locations throughout Québec and Ontario. In addition to its Workhorse offerings, the company is also an authorized Michelin tire, Cummins engine, and Vanguard trailer dealer.
