#4397. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 23, 2026

This week has been home to some disheartening news. BioWare, the creators of games like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, is being shut down amid a flurry of layoffs. It's another frustrating story from a struggling video game industry. Below you will find some of our stories about the legendary developer, including our massive 2016 oral history. And then after that, you can read about our recommendations of what to play this weekend.

I spent the early hours playing Final Fantasy Resonance trying to figure out precisely why I couldn't put it down. I eventually realized that the game manages in a very purposeful way to answer that quiet need I've so frequently had: "I wish I could experience a game just like Final Fantasy IV or VI again, for the first time, but with a new cast and story." That's pretty much what you can expect here; Resonance is a very purposeful throwback experience that harkens to the early days of FF pixel adventures, but with several modern conveniences, graphical flourishes, and depth added into the mix. It's a big and refreshingly wholesome journey of entertaining party members, summoning giant creatures, flying an airship across the world, and fighting turn-based battles that include absurd spell effects. It's one of my favorite games of the year, and well worth the time it will take to explore. Read our full review for more.

Expect to hear a lot of people proclaiming this as "one of the good ones," as Modern Warfare came out swinging this week with a strong campaign, compelling additions to competitive multiplayer, and an impressive extraction shooter mode in the form of DMZ. I've already been impressed by the first few hours of the campaign, which offers a tense, harrowing, and often disturbingly brutal story that bounces between a number of character perspectives. The gunplay feels tuned in, the traversal and melee is satisfying, and the narrative beats grounded in excellent actin performances. Our reviewer has spent even more time with the full game, and can share their full perspective to help inform whether you want to take a dive into this year's installment.

The Nintendo Sports franchise, which began with Wii Sports in 2006, has never been about the single-player experience. That remains true 20 years later in Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. But this time around, Nintendo has boosted the amount of content beyond what the series has typically provided, appealing to all player counts, all while retaining its trademark approachability. Whether you're joining together with three friends for some friendly competition across the package's 12 sports or you're trying to climb the Island Crown ladder by beating increasingly difficult single-player opponents, Switch Sports Resort is a great motion-controlled collection.

Halloween is around the corner. As you’re buying overpriced candy, deciding which version of the Joker to dress up as, and debating between watching Obsession and Backrooms over a cup of cider, it’s the perfect time to replay old horror games or dive into new ones. 2026 has a solid roster of choices for the latter thanks to releases like Resident Evil Requiem, Paranormasight: The Mermaid’s Curse, and Silent Hill: Townfall, but Tenebris Somnia shouldn’t be overlooked if you’re looking for a cool indie throwback.

Part retro-inspired adventure game, part live-action indie horror film, you’ll uncover the mystery of a nightmare-induced apartment building and battle horrors to rescue your trapped ex. The gameplay is survival horror 101, but it’s executed well, with consistently clever and inventive puzzle-solving as a highlight. It may not be a graphical powerhouse, but Tenebris Somnia still maintains a creepy atmosphere thanks to solid scares partly delivered by effective and well-made live-action cinematics. If you’re going to binge horror films, you may as well play one too. You can read my full review here.

Full disclosure: I have not played One Piece: Grand Gourmet. I was trying to finish up Castlevania: Belmont's Curse when a review game landed in my lap that I've had to give my full attention. That said, I have watched a lot of the One Piece anime, have a cat named Nami, and dog named Luffy.

I don't know if One Piece: Grand Gourmet is any good, but I like the premise and pixel graphics. One Piece is a very malleable franchise (which is why its live action adaptation is pretty good), so the idea of managing a restaurant as Sanji feels like it could be a very good fit. I plan on climbing aboard with all my hopes and dreams soon. And it is out now, which is good to know.

Similar to the entry above, I have not yet played Stupid Never Dies yet (there are too many video games!), but we like to use this weekly article to call out the new video games of the week. I am eager to check out Stupid Never Dies primarily because of its pop-punk soundtrack and 2000s aesthetic. I think it has the potential to be a fun, nostalgic throwback to my youth when I was learning Blink-182's "Dammit" on guitar and playing Devil May Cry.

The Blood of Dawnwalker has been out for just over seven weeks now, but I wouldn't blame you if you haven't finished it – or even started it – yet. A lot has come out! But if you need a reason to jump back in, this week's 1.1 update is a great excuse – the devs have added hundreds of bug fixes and other minor improvements, so it should run better than it ever did before. There's also an even easier difficulty mode if you want to cruise through without worrying about combat, and a new in-game potion that lets you respec all your skill points. I stalled out about halfway through (when I started playing Wolverine), but I'm planning to jump back in this weekend.

Oh, and you can pet dogs and cats now. Maybe I should have led with that.

Multiplayer physics mountain-climbing game Peak became one of the most viral co-op experiences of 2025 (I refuse to use the term friendslop), but only PC players have enjoyed its wacky shenanigans. That changed this week as Peak is now available on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Switch 2. Either alone or, preferably, alongside up to three friends, you’ll try to ascend procedurally generated, absurdly unrealistic mountains riddled with dangers. Working together is key, a tricky prospect thanks to the in-game proximity chat that necessitates sticking together, but griefing each other, intentionally or otherwise, is just as entertaining – maddeningly frustrating at times, but entertaining. Peak on consoles includes all post-launch content and, best of all, supports crossplay for all platforms.

The original Azul remains one of my all-time favorite games even after many years, but it just misses the bar with its strategic complexity to be one I'd pull out to play with the kids. That why I was especially delighted to find that Azul Kids is one of those rare "adapted for children" projects that turned out extremely well.

Players take on the roll of creative young artists building mosaic displays with various colored tiles. The concept remains simple enough to work for even very young players of age five or six, but the whole family should have fun with the approachable strategy implications of choosing tiles and completing your masterpiece.

#4396. Battlefield 6 patch finally ends the menace of the Lock-Guided Missile, shuts down the Recon Drone Sledgehammer exploit and more

Today's Battlefield 6 patch is laser-focused on taking care of some of the more infuriating bugs while also taking out a couple of exploits.

The next Battlefield 6 update is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the issues that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an issue that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

Patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.

#4395. Arc Raiders has proven that extraction shooters can be popular, with over 4 million copies sold in under two weeks

Arc Raiders has sold even more copies, which we should've guessed, given that the game keeps breaking its own concurrent player records.

It’s pretty clear at this stage that Arc Raiders is one of the biggest launches of 2025. More interesting than the numbers themselves, however, is that this is an extraction shooter - a subgenre which has typically been thought of as niche.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Today, publisher Nexon announced in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

The news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios announced that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s currently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

“The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

Just over the weekend, the game received several new Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

If you’re currently hooked on this gem of a game, we guarantee that our Arc Raiders gameplay tips will have at least one you didn’t know about. We also have more guides on how to find some of the more elusive items in the game, such as olives, lemons and apricots, and prickly pears.

#4394. MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body

MIT researchers have developed a new technique that allows them to transform immune cells into cancer fighters directly inside the body, potentially making advanced treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases much easier to produce and administer.

The method focuses on natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell that can be engineered to recognize and destroy harmful cells. These include cancerous T cells and T cells that mistakenly attack healthy tissue, contributing to conditions such as lymphoma and autoimmune hepatitis.

Rather than extracting immune cells from a patient and modifying them in a laboratory, the researchers use tiny particles made of fatty molecules to deliver genetic instructions directly to NK cells. These instructions, carried by messenger RNA, tell the cells to produce specialized proteins that help them identify and eliminate diseased T cells.

The resulting cells, known as CAR NK cells, could eventually be used against several different diseases. By carrying out the engineering process inside the body, the new approach could eliminate much of the time, expense, and complexity involved in manufacturing personalized immune cell therapies.

"The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells," says Daniel Anderson, a professor in MIT's Department of Chemical Engineering and a member of MIT's Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science.

Anderson is the senior author of the research, published in Nature Biotechnology. The lead authors are MIT postdoctoral researcher Yuang Chen and graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal. Robert Langer, MIT's David H. Koch Institute Professor, also contributed to the study.

Why Current Cancer Immunotherapies Are So Complex

Immune cell engineering has already transformed treatment options for certain cancers. During the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven cancer therapies that use genetically modified T cells, known as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells.

These treatments work by equipping T cells with specially designed receptors that recognize particular markers, or antigens, on other cells. When an engineered T cell encounters its designated target, such as a protein associated with cancer, it becomes activated and attacks the cell carrying that marker.

CAR T cell therapies have been especially effective against blood cancers arising from B cells. These include certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma, as well as multiple myeloma.

However, preparing these treatments involves several complicated steps. Doctors first collect blood from the patient and send it to a specialized facility. There, technicians separate the T cells, genetically modify them to produce the desired receptors, and grow enough engineered cells for treatment. The finished cells must then be transported back to the hospital and infused into the patient.

Natural Killer Cells Offer a Different Way to Fight Cancer

Scientists have recently been exploring whether natural killer cells could be engineered in a similar way. One important advantage is their potential to treat cancers and autoimmune conditions involving abnormal T cells.

Trying to use CAR T cells against diseased T cells creates a major problem. Because both the engineered cells and their intended targets are T cells, the modified cells may recognize and destroy one another. This unintended attack can undermine the treatment.

Natural killer cells avoid this complication because they are a different type of immune cell. They can be programmed to attack harmful T cells without triggering the same problem of engineered T cells killing each other.

"NK cells can treat these T cell malignancies -- not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases," Chen says.

Producing CAR NK cells outside the body, however, still requires much of the specialized equipment, labor, and processing associated with CAR T cell manufacturing. To overcome these limitations, the MIT team investigated whether NK cells could instead be engineered "in vivo," meaning directly inside the body.

"If a patient can just get an infusion of nanoparticles, it would dramatically simplify the process and reduce costs," Anderson says.

Although researchers are actively developing CAR NK cell therapies for cancer and autoimmune disorders, none have received FDA approval.

How mRNA Nanoparticles Reprogram Immune Cells

The MIT team designed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) capable of transporting messenger RNA into natural killer cells. The mRNA carries instructions for producing a chimeric antigen receptor that directs the modified immune cell toward a specific target.

The technology can be adapted to recognize different proteins depending on the disease being treated. For example, the researchers can provide instructions for a receptor that recognizes CD19, a protein found on B cells, or CD3, a protein present on T cells, including those responsible for autoimmune attacks.

To help the nanoparticles reach the correct immune cells, the scientists covered their surfaces with antibody fragments. These fragments recognize and attach to receptors on NK cells, helping deliver the genetic instructions where they are needed.

Once inside an NK cell, the mRNA directs the production of the new receptor, giving the immune cell the ability to recognize and attack its intended target.

The researchers then tested whether this approach could efficiently reprogram NK cells and whether the resulting cells could combat cancer and autoimmune disease in mice.

Reprogrammed Immune Cells Eliminate Tumors in Mice

The initial experiments produced encouraging results. After injecting the nanoparticles into mice, the researchers successfully modified approximately 80 percent of the NK cells they were targeting.

They next investigated whether these engineered cells could attack tumors. In mice with an aggressive form of melanoma, three of the five animals treated with nanoparticles designed to direct NK cells against the cancer experienced complete remission.

The researchers also tested the technique against T cell lymphoma using humanized mice. These animals receive transfusions of human blood cells, temporarily giving them immune systems that share certain characteristics with those of humans.

In this model, the treatment produced substantial tumor destruction. After five injections of the nanoparticles, the tumors were completely eliminated.

Importantly, these results were comparable to those achieved with CAR NK cells produced through the more traditional method of collecting NK cells, modifying them outside the body, and then returning them to the animals.

This suggests that generating CAR NK cells directly inside the body could offer similar cancer-fighting capabilities while avoiding the complicated manufacturing process required by conventional cell therapies.

A Single Injection Reverses Autoimmune Liver Damage

The researchers also wanted to determine whether their technology could help treat autoimmune diseases, in which the immune system mistakenly damages healthy tissues.

They focused on autoimmune hepatitis, a condition in which abnormal T cells attack hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver. By designing nanoparticles that instruct NK cells to recognize these harmful T cells, the scientists tested whether they could interrupt the autoimmune response.

The treatment successfully eliminated the autoreactive T cells in mice with the disease. Even more encouragingly, the animals' damaged liver tissue healed after the harmful immune cells were removed.

These improvements occurred after just one nanoparticle injection, demonstrating the potential of the approach beyond cancer treatment.

"This study is an excellent example of the power of nano delivery systems and their ability to potentially treat cancer and other diseases," Langer says.

A New Direction for Cancer and Autoimmune Treatments

The researchers believe that reprogramming natural killer cells inside the body could eventually provide new treatment options for a much wider range of conditions.

Among the diseases they hope to target are multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, both of which can involve harmful immune responses driven by dysfunctional T cells.

Although the findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and further research will be necessary to determine whether the technique is safe and effective in humans.

If successful, the technology could make engineered immune cell treatments considerably more accessible by replacing a lengthy laboratory manufacturing process with the direct delivery of genetic instructions through nanoparticles.

The research received funding from Sanofi, the Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine, and a Koch Institute Support (core) Grant from the National Cancer Institute.

#4393. Phantom Blade Zero Review In Progress – Shaping Up To Be One Of The Best Action Games I've Ever Played

Phantom Blade Zero is an astounding achievement for the action genre. So astounding that I feel pulled to experience everything it has to offer… and that means instead of rolling credits, I’ve been busy completing story-critical side quests and more to get the most complete ending. That’s another way of saying I am enjoying this game very, very much but still need more time to render a final verdict, which is why you’re reading a review-in-progress of Phantom Blade Zero rather than a scored piece.

Though I’m not interested in guesstimating a score right now, I know it will be high because Phantom Blade Zero impresses and then some. It is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and I’m shocked to be writing that. This is a debut of sorts for developer S-Game, which has dabbled in mobile games and smaller-scale titles; it’s the team’s first triple-A release, and its first game of this kind. This studio is so clearly a dedicated student of the genre, analyzing what works here and what works there in other action greats to create something of its own. It looks forward at what action games can do, can play like, can look like, while looking back at the games before it and understanding why those games – games like Devil May Cry, Elden Ring, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Bayonetta, and just about every other quality action game you can think of – continue to be ones we hold so highly. Should it stick the landing, Phantom Blade Zero will join that echelon of action pedigree.

Protagonist Soul is a quiet, mostly stoic martial arts master who prefers to let his blades (of which there are so, so many) do the talking. The Order he’s sworn his life to betrays him, and, in an effort to right wrongs, he discovers a villainous conspiracy to seize full power of the blood-soaked Chinese martial underground known as Wulin. As a result, puppets, secret sects, powerful god-like creatures, monstrous beasts, and much more prowl Wulin’s various biomes. I haven’t kept count, but there are a massive number of enemies to take down, both standard mob variants and bosses, and the game stays fresh throughout. It's even fresher when you consider how many weapons you can acquire on Soul’s journey.

Every weapon is wholly unique, like picking up a new character in a fighting game, each with its own moveset and abilities. Upgrading these weapons through various tiers unlocks additional abilities, and you can even Soul Temper weapons to add one final, game-changing ability or perk. A fully upgraded weapon can have a moveset that uses the majority of buttons on your controller. You can do the same with Phantom Edges, special tide-turning weapons with limited uses (before you build up additional charges). Combined with different accessories and medicine types, Phantom Blade Zero offers hundreds, perhaps thousands, of combat kit permutations. You can play as a drunken fighter who switches between sober, tipsy, and drunken states, with his range and damage output changing as a result; you can focus on a bleed build, ripping enemies to shreds with charged attacks that utilize Soul's own HP to deal extra damage (that can then be earned back with bleed); you can use lightning, wind, fire, and ice to create elemental storms against enemies, and you can use a sword that switches between different elemental states on command as well. You can also just pound enemies to pulp with Phantom Edge fists, too. I’ve struggled to stop using these fists since acquiring them because they’re so satisfying.

Forty-plus hours into Phantom Blade Zero, it feels like I’ve played as dozens of different Souls because I've discovered so many build types. S-Game smartly pushes you to try new builds and weapons as you get them, doling out generous upgrade materials and currency; it encourages you to try everything, and the next weapon might just become your new favorite.

Finding these materials (and additional fights) is great fun, too, because Phantom Blade Zero’s various open-area biomes are a genuine joy to explore. You are always rewarded for taking the optional path, and those rewards are always worthwhile. You might find a healthy pile of upgrade materials, or a boss with a weapon you’ll fall in love with. The way buildings, alleys, caves, cliffsides, and other environmental features weave in and out of each other evokes FromSoftware’s architectural design and the subsequent shortcut “aha!” moments.

That said, Phantom Blade Zero is definitively not a Soulslike, though you’d be forgiven for assuming as much given its challenging suite of bosses, interconnected world, and Phantom Bell checkpoints, which are this game’s equivalent of bonfires. However, its challenge is much more surmountable (with various difficulties and accessories to ease parry and dodge timing), and its world progression is materially different. Kill an enemy and it’s dead for good, which to my surprise, adds a sense of worldbuilding I didn’t know I wanted. Progression through this journey feels tangible because I’m actually removing traces of evil with my weapons, traces that don’t respawn when I interact with checkpoints. It’s a nice change of pace that narratively speaks to Soul’s efforts.

Along the way, countless reading materials shed light on Phantom Blade Zero’s intertwining stories, and tracking down the next memory, scroll, or book entry rewards you if you’re interested in the full picture of this Wuxia story. I’d argue the game’s story is its weakest element, but only when compared to the rest of the package. It doesn't break any new ground narratively, but it provides enough mystery and thrill to keep things moving. And while performances are great, talking to characters is still mostly just two people standing across from each other talking through a new quest. Fortunately, cutscenes pick up the slack with dramatic villains, heartfelt revelations, raw tension, and more.

Production value is high across the board, thanks to incredibly impressive animation and a beautiful rendering of this dark fantasy China. Faces are lifelike, nudging up just shy of the uncanny valley as close-ups reveal porous details, lip quivers, and more, bringing an excellent cast of Chinese performances to life. The English voice acting has its standouts, but Soul’s voice is boring, so I highly recommend the Chinese vocals.

Boss fights draw clear inspiration from Chinese cinema and boast a wondrous sense of awe and scale that only the best in the genre typically offer. There are a ton of bosses, too, with very few repeats (repeats do happen in segmented challenge trials), and it’s impressive to think back on just how many I defeated, and just how many of them delivered a unique fight. I appreciate the checkpoints between boss phases as well. There are so many bosses – nearing 100 or more if I had to guess – and having my progression saved through phases removes some of the repetition I often feel when, say, phase two of a boss continues to kill me and I have to blitz through phase one again and again before taking another stab at it.

That scale and on-screen excitement carry through almost every fight in the game, down to even the simplest mob fights, though these are starting to feel a touch repetitive as I’m barreling toward the game’s end. Soul moves like the world’s greatest martial artist, but your controller inputs make it happen. If you mash the attack button, it looks nice… but if you use each weapon’s prescribed inputs and abilities, Phantom Blade Zero delivers a level of detailed action I’ve seen in few other games. You direct the game’s action, and this lets you turn what might otherwise be just another group of fodder enemies into an electric bout of spectacle.

To say I greatly enjoy this game greatly undersells my feelings – writing this review-in-progress is frustrating because I want to get back to Phantom Blade Zero. I expect to reach credits in the coming days, so please be on the lookout for my final verdict this week.

#4392. 10 Biggest Reveals From Final Fantasy 14's Tokyo Fanfest

Stephanie Watel is a writer for DualShockers. She has 3 years of experience writing about video games, from news to lists to in-depth guides.

To be perfectly candid, Final Fantasy XIV’s Tokyo leg of the Fanfest circuit ahead of Evercold was a surreal and almost puzzling experience. Most of the expansion’s biggest surprises were already spoiled in both Anaheim and Berlin, while Tokyo essentially served as a clarity-and-elaboration session for much of what we already knew in a basic sense.

However, that isn’t to say that director Naoki (“Yoshi-P”) Yoshida’s keynote wasn’t full of impressively dense information for players to soak in. There was a lot to go around, to the point that Yoshi-P went almost 30 minutes past his allotted runtime for the presentation, on top of saying that it originally came out to almost four hours during rehearsal. That still doesn’t even include the “several” Producer Live Letter streams he also has planned leading up to Evercold’s launch to go over everything even further.

Square Enix veteran Koji Fox says lead writer Natsuko Ishikawa is snowed under and off-limits.

If anything, it’s a perfect metaphor for just how dramatically different Evercold is actually set to be, compared to all previous expansions in the game. Most of the game’s major content is getting a systemic overhaul, and those changes branch out even further, down to some of the smallest details. It’s almost on par with A Realm Reborn’s aptly named “rebirth” of the entire game over a decade ago, without having to shut the entire game down for nearly a year.

All that said, Tokyo Fanfest had plenty of information for players to take with them, and here are the biggest reveals from the entire keynote.

Evercold dropping in the dead of winter in January was poetically on point, and up through Berlin’s Fanfest we’ve known that Final Fantasy 14’s latest and most ambitious expansion yet was set to kick off a busy year for gamers (with the likes of Fable and Final Fantasy 7: Revelation also set for early Spring).

However, at the top of Yoshi-P’s keynote in Tokyo, he announced with regret that Evercold has gotten a three-week delay to late February. Now the expansion will debut on February 23, 2027, with a special Early Access period for those who pre-order starting on February 19.

As for why this is the case, Yoshi-P explained that, initially, Evercold would have been “barely” ready to go in time for their original January release deadline, which going by a three-week delay means that the expansion would have arrived at the tail end of month. However, due to “several issues” they encountered during development, Yoshi-P made the executive decision to impose the delay to ensure those problems are properly resolved before launch.

Despite this, the delay hasn’t impacted when players will get to preorder Evercold, and you can do so for all platforms starting November 4, 2026. Ultimately, given just how much is changing in the game systemically with Evercold, it’s just as well that this delay happened, and January did seem a bit ambitious already. Nonetheless, the rock isn’t getting kicked too far down the street, and the expansion will be in players’ hands soon enough.

On the heels of Evercold’s amended release date announcement, Yoshi-P pivoted straight to the grand reveal of the expansion’s second new combat job. Granted, there was strong speculation already after the many hints dropped at Berlin’s Fanfest that it revolved around something akin to a Hunter or a Falconer, and it was already confirmed that it would be a physical ranged DPS.

Finally, all the theory crafting was laid to rest with the reveal of Zephyr, courtesy of Visna posing as the job’s mascot. As shown in the active demonstration video, the player wields a crossbow weapon while flanked by a magical falcon familiar known as a Nephele. The video displayed various combat abilities, from basic attacks with the crossbow to more striking, magic-imbued ones that have your work together with your falcon to produce some spectacular moves.

What’s more, during a Q&A session on the second day of Tokyo’s Fanfest, Yoshi-P answered a fan’s question about being able to customize your bird companion. It turns out that you actually can thanks to a dual-dye system that allows you to recolor the bird when visiting a “certain NPC” in the game.

While FF14 players knew that changes to gear would be inevitable with Evercold’s new activity system, Yoshi-P surprised just about everyone during the keynote with sweeping alterations to raid gear in particular.

While Seasonal Gear is intended for “everyday” players with a simple optimization routine, Raid Gear comes with a few different new details. The first and most surprising change is that every single person in a raid group will now get their own personal chest drop after completing the duty, rather than having the group roll the dice on a single chest once a week. This will make raiding significantly more efficient (especially for premade groups or “statics”) in lieu of having to farm several runs just for the sake of gearing everyone up for the next raid.

Alongside that, players will also get to edit the “secondary attributes” of raid gear, allowing them to personally customize how their earned gear performs rather than just being stuck with preset attributes. Also, the item level of Raid Gear can be raised twice, and materia slots will unlock upon reaching that maximum item level.

Yoshi-P went into explicit detail in this section of the keynote to explain exactly how the gear upgrading process will work, and while it felt somewhat like a labyrinth of steps and stat numbers, it nonetheless looks like a promising move in the right direction for the game’s raid community in general.

The core that’s tying mostly everything together in Evercold’s revamped gameplay is the all-new Activity Level system. The Berlin keynote gave a soft introduction to this system with a basic explanation of weekly missions that will replace Final Fantasy 14’s traditional daily duties.

During the Tokyo keynote, Yoshi-P tied that back in with the introduction of the Activity Level system, which is how all players will obtain their Seasonal Gear throughout each “season” of the expansion’s patch cycle. As you complete Missions from the long list of available options, you’ll earn Activity Points that in turn raise your Activity Level. As that level goes up, you’ll gradually unlock rewards for your efforts, ranging from gil to emotes to mounts, and then so-called “gear categories”.

Unlocking these gear categories allows you to receive gear pieces of that category (e.g. - accessories) for your jobs. Furthermore, each category is shared across all jobs, so you don’t have to worry about your alt jobs missing out on those rewards. Redeeming those gear rewards is also done via the game’s new character UI dashboard.

Up to this point, the basic understanding that we have about our journey on the Fourth is that most of it will occur on the planet’s Fimm Himnar realmships, or the “Five Firmaments Left to Mankind”. These absolutely massive realmships each pertain to a different element and a certain sector of produced resources that can’t otherwise be obtained on the frozen surface.

Back in the Berlin Fanfest, Yoshi-P provided a detailed look at two of these realmships. One was Naglfar, the Realmship of Water where Visna resides. The other was Hringhorni, the Realmship of Fire where we now know that Bastion-wielding Baldr serves as its foreman.

Here's everything you need to know Final Fantasy XIV Evercold, from new characters, new factions, and how we're able to travel to different shards.

This time around, in-depth looks were provided for two more of these realmships. One was the Realmship of Earth, Sessrymnir, and a walkthrough video gave insight into the ship’s agriculture and mining production areas. Meanwhile, the Realmship of Wind, Skidbladnir, was also shown off in all its glory. Not only is it where the ridiculously adorable Kottr live, but it’s where they work on the production of airships, the main method of transportation on the Fourth.

The fifth and final realmship remains a mystery, which is likely for the sake of story spoilers, and it also remains to be seen what other explorable areas there may be. After all, a traditional Final Fantasy XIV expansion normally has at least six major zones that players can freely navigate, and the five realmships leave at least one of those zones in limbo. The closest guess would be somewhere on the subzero surface of the Fourth, but players will have to wait and see in February.

Alliance Raids aren’t just getting a new collaboration with Neon Genesis Evangelion for Evercold, they’re also getting their own systemic overhaul for the new expansion and beyond. These changes, according to Yoshi-P, reflect a few overarching issues that the content has suffered from over past expansions.

These issues start with skewed runtimes for the game’s entire roster of Alliance Raids. Some are generally more “efficient” to run, while others (e.g. - Tower of Paradigm’s Reach) are notoriously long and thus considered not optimal for dailies, leveling, farming gear, what have you. This gaping divide in runtime has since led to a bias within the player community, and leaves certain Alliance Raids infamously difficult to queue for, much less actually complete.

However, Yoshi-P has sought out a solution in the form of subdividing Alliance Raids into two instanced chunks. The first chunk will consist of the overall raid’s first two bosses (with trash mobs in between), while the second chunk will be the final two bosses in the same fashion. After completing the first half and obtaining your rewards from it, you’ll then be able to queue separately at your own discretion for the second half, complete it, and earn separate rewards from that chunk.

This is to help alleviate the burden of farming endlessly for certain gear items over the course of a 30 minute to 1 hour raid instance, all while also being able to enjoy the content more feasibly with less of a time commitment. Furthermore, Yoshi-P hinted at not having to roll anymore for loot from these raids, with a promise to elaborate more on that closer to Evercold’s launch.

Finally, Alliance Raids get one more big update starting in Evercold in the form of a legitimate “Savage” mode. Influenced by the success of Variant and Criterion Dungeon content, this will be an 8-player mode, rather than the usual lineup of 24 WoLs, and will function more as a boss rush-style instance with two bosses from the original raid set at “Savage Turn 3”-level difficulty. This mode will kick off with Evercold’s Evangelion collaboration raid series.

While many of the game’s existing combat modes are getting their own unique changes, there’s also an entirely new type of combat content debuting during Evercold called the Gauntlet of Power.

As its name suggests, it’s a gauntlet-style instance that functions as a more casual (compared to Alliance Raid Savage, at least) boss rush for players to embark on at their leisure. That is to say, it’s a mode that can be easily accessed from almost anywhere via the game’s overhauled UI. It can be played either with a premade group or a random queue, in much the same fashion as other instanced duties in the game.

This boss rush consists of up to five “floors” for a light party group, and clearing each floor leads to rewards that weren’t yet revealed during the keynote. Players can vote whether or not to continue the gauntlet, which provides a flexibility that not many of the other types of battle content in the game have. Despite being simple in concept, it may very well help bridge a gap that’s been lingering in Final Fantasy’s 14 gameplay flow for several years.

What’s more, this mode will help keep things interesting by choosing from an assortment of 200 different existing bosses in the game. This assures that the mode will traditionally prevalent issue of content monotony as much as possible while maintaining a sense of liberty and gratification for the player to make the most of their time.

Another big surprise that Yoshi-P was surprisingly candid about during Tokyo Fanfest’s Q&A session is that Allagan Tomestones of Poetics, the currency that’s remained in the game the longest (aside from maybe MGP), is set to officially retire in Evercold.

Yoshi-P did say that he shouldn’t really be discussing it just yet, but did confirm the plan nonetheless. He did offer a brief explanation in that “there will be something that allows you to trade for gear for alt jobs, or past rewards; you don’t have to worry about it for now. It just won’t be Poetics anymore.”

For players who have been in Final Fantasy 14 for at least some amount of time, Allagan Tomestones has since become the fall-back currency for the game’s more niche purchases. Alternatively, you could redeem them for one of the game’s more recent variants of tomestone currencies. Beyond A Realm Reborn, Poetics lose much of their remaining purpose, and at this point they feel more like a souvenir that just collects dust from one expansion to the next.

However, on that note, with the game’s dramatic revamp to the Activity Points system and Seasonal Gear, it remains to be seen if other tomestone currencies, such as those we had in Dawntrail, will keep some sort of utility themselves. Yoshi-P hasn’t been abundantly clear on just how long tomestone currency will hang on for, and if it will perhaps deviate to some other set purpose in the game. Otherwise, Evercold may be the “poetic” farewell to tomestone currency across the board as we know it.

While not necessarily anything to do with the game’s many different content systems, the keynote did get a small update on the story front in the form of identity reveals for certain characters. Baldr, the one wielding Bastion gear in the trailer, was revealed as the foreman of the Hringhorni realmship. Meanwhile, an entirely new face appeared in the final version of the trailer that ironically looked very familiar to many fans.

The presentation revealed her as Lagertha, the first mate of the Naglfar realmship where Visna resides. However, beyond finding out her purpose on the ship, fans are moreso scratching their heads over her striking resemblance to Ysayle, a key character who tragically passed during the events of Heavensward and the Dragonsong War.

However, players with a sharp eye may have caught the glimpse of her during the final Dawntrail MSQ content in Patch 7.56, meaning that her appearance is no coincidence. The most likely explanation for her presence on the Fourth is that Lagertha is her reflection. As to how deeply her character will impact the story of Evercold, players will simply have to wait and look forward to it.

On another non-combat tangent, Final Fantasy 14’s ever-controversial housing system is getting more bells and whistles added to it with Evercold’s patch cycle. Those changes are spread across “three pillars”, as indicated in the presentation.

First off, as hinted over the past several months, all houses will get an “interior area size customization” feature. This means that, for example, you can customize the interior of your small house to have the layout of a large house, for a currently undisclosed gil fee. Not only that, the furnishing limit will flex according to the layout you choose, so there’s no need to worry about getting cut off on your desired decor.

Secondly, floating interior furnishings will no longer be something only achievable through unconventional PC glitching controls. Along with an all-new placement interface, players will be able to move furnishings more freely on the vertical axis on both console and PC platforms.

The third and final pillar consists of adding even more housing plots, though Yoshi-P noted that they’re still discussing how exactly they want to achieve that, whether it’s through more, smaller areas, “hidden” areas, et cetera. While more plots feels moreso like another bandaid to a system that itself needs an overhaul, it’s at least nice that they’re doing their best to improve what’s in place until that change hopefully comes one day.

Breaking New Ground is the name of that event, and it’s one where everyone will need to contribute in order to rebuild some old tunnels and unlock the way to Stella Montis.

#4389. A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut

A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible. New preclinical research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center reveals how fasting and beneficial microbes work together to activate the body's natural tissue repair mechanisms.

The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment. By improving the intestine's ability to recover from radiation exposure, researchers hope to reduce serious side effects and potentially make radiation therapy safer and more effective.

Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine.

"Fasting helps prepare intestinal cells to respond more quickly and effectively after injury, almost like training the cells with an emergency preparedness plan," Piwnica-Worms said. "This study helps explain how that plan is organized and identifies a key bacterium involved in coordinating the response."

Why Radiation Therapy Can Damage the Intestines

Radiation therapy is widely used to treat cancers in the abdomen, including pancreatic, colorectal, and gynecologic cancers. Although radiation can destroy cancer cells, it can also harm nearby healthy tissue. The small intestine is particularly vulnerable because its delicate lining is highly sensitive to radiation exposure.

When this protective lining becomes damaged, patients may experience nausea, diarrhea, and infections. Severe injuries can cause life-threatening complications. These risks can also restrict the amount of radiation doctors can safely administer, potentially limiting treatment options.

Previous preclinical research from the Piwnica-Worms Laboratory showed that fasting before radiation exposure helped the intestines recover afterward. However, researchers had not fully determined why going without food produced this protective effect.

The latest study provides an important piece of that puzzle by identifying a specific gut bacterium and explaining how it helps intestinal cells prepare for injury.

Researchers found that 24 hours of fasting increased the abundance of a beneficial bacterium called Akkermansia muciniphila, also known as AKK, in the small intestine. This microbe produces a substance called propionate, which helps trigger changes inside intestinal cells that make them better prepared to regenerate following radiation damage.

Propionate works alongside other metabolic changes caused by fasting to modify proteins known as histones. These proteins serve as structures around which DNA is packaged inside cells. Small chemical markers added to histones can influence which genes become active without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

These modifications make portions of DNA more accessible, allowing cells to activate genes involved in tissue regeneration. During fasting, a population of intestinal cells carrying these repair programs becomes more abundant.

In effect, fasting helps prepare these cells with the biological instructions they will need if an injury occurs. When the intestines are subsequently exposed to radiation, the prepared cells can expand and help rebuild the damaged intestinal lining.

One Gut Bacterium Proves Essential for Recovery

To determine how important AKK was to this process, the researchers selectively removed the bacterium. Without it, fasting no longer produced the same regenerative benefits.

Even more revealing, the protective response returned only when the bacterium was restored in combination with fasting. This demonstrated that neither component alone was sufficient to reproduce the full effect observed in the study.

The results suggest that fasting does more than temporarily change the gut's metabolism. Together with AKK, it alters the activity of intestinal cells before radiation exposure, placing them in a state that supports more efficient recovery after damage occurs.

By uncovering this connection between nutrition, gut bacteria, and cellular regeneration, the researchers have identified a potential new way to strengthen the body's response to tissue injury. The discovery could be especially valuable for protecting healthy organs during cancer treatment.

Could Gut Bacteria Make Cancer Treatment Safer?

Although the results are promising, the research remains preclinical. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether the same protective mechanism operates in humans and whether it can safely improve outcomes for patients receiving radiation therapy.

One possibility is that the newly discovered pathway could be used to help other healthy tissues recover from cancer treatment. Researchers are particularly interested in tissues with rapidly dividing cells, including bone marrow, which can also suffer treatment-related damage.

If further investigations support the findings, clinical trials could eventually explore whether activating this repair mechanism benefits patients undergoing abdominal radiation therapy.

Importantly, the discovery may also provide ways to achieve these effects without requiring patients to fast. Treatments involving beneficial bacteria or the molecules they produce could potentially stimulate similar repair processes while avoiding the practical difficulties of food restriction during cancer care.

"Fasting is not always practical for cancer patients, and this work supports several other potential ways to enhance recovery after treatment," Rai said. "Whether through dietary interventions, targeted microbes or their metabolites, the goal is to help repair healthy tissue more effectively while patients receive the cancer therapies they need."

The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT).

Materials provided by University of Texas M. D. Anderson Cancer Center. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4388. Battlefield 6 gets a new map today alongside major changes to controller aim assist, and even more weapon dispersion tweaks

Right on schedule, the latest Battlefield 6 patch has arrived to kick off the next stage of Season 1.

Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major update earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The update, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

We’ve known about the new content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The update kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

There’s a new limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other big new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

These are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

Redsec players have a new Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a big overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

Controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this update, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several issues that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

#4387. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with... a questionable selection of maps, but at least the modes are good

If Redsec got you hooked on Battlefield gameplay but you never experienced traditional multiplayer in Battlefield 6, there's an upcoming moment you might want to pay attention to.

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

As for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for new players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

#4386. After EA, Silver Lake and PIF Reportedly Want Unity

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

Unity Software has held talks to be acquired by a consortium that includes private equity firm Silver Lake and Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, according to Reuters. The group discussed a valuation of around $25 billion, whilst Unity’s market cap sits at roughly $21.5 billion after its latest earnings report. Shares rose about 4% in extended trading once the story broke.

Nothing is certain. The approach came in recent weeks, and Unity has reportedly been working with an investment bank to weigh its options ever since. Reuters notes that the plan and terms could still change, and Unity declined to comment.

Silver Lake and PIF have done this before. Both were part of the consortium behind the $55 billion EA take-private that closed in August, which ranks among the largest leveraged buyouts ever. A Unity deal would be their second enormous gaming bet in a matter of months.

Silver Lake isn’t walking in cold, either. It invested up to $400 million in Unity back in 2017 and still owns around 8% of the company. Its Egon Durban sits on Unity’s board, a dual role that would normally see him recuse himself from any board discussion of a sale. That’s the kind of detail that looks tidy on paper and gets picked at later.

Most people know Unity as the engine behind thousands of mobile, console and PC games, but its reach goes further than that. It’s used in automotive design, filmmaking, architecture and industrial simulation too. The company started out in Denmark in 2004, went public in September 2020, and has since wandered into advertising technology.

That advertising side is currently pulling its weight. Unity’s third quarter beat estimates, with revenue up 32% to $622.1 million and adjusted earnings of 44 cents per share. Strong growth in its AI-powered Vector platform helped it post its first quarterly profit on a GAAP basis since the IPO, alongside a solid showing from its game-development business. The takeover report landed straight afterwards. A company that has just turned its first profit is a much easier sell to a buyer, and I doubt that’s a coincidence.

There’s a practical angle too. According to Reuters, Unity’s tools are already used by Scopely, the developer behind Monopoly Go!, and Niantic, the creator of Pokémon Go, both of which are owned by a group that includes PIF, Silver Lake and Affinity Partners. The buyers would be acquiring something their own studios already rely on.

PIF’s route into gaming mostly runs through Savvy Games Group, which has had a mandate to invest $38 billion in the sector since 2022. Savvy bought Scopely for $4.9 billion in 2023, and Scopely then bought Niantic’s games business, Pokémon Go included, for $3.5 billion. ESL and FACEIT sit under the same umbrella. In January, PIF moved around $12 billion in listed gaming shares across to Savvy, including its stakes in Nintendo and Bandai Namco, followed by its roughly $3 billion Take-Two stake a month later. Add the EA deal on top and the list of major publishers with no Saudi money attached gets shorter every year.

The group discussed a valuation of around $25 billion, whilst Unity’s market cap sits at roughly $21.5 billion after its latest earnings report.

Savvy’s chief, Brian Ward, said at GDC that it doesn’t plan to use those stakes to push publishers into big changes. Taking him at his word, a minority shareholder is one thing. Owning the engine that other studios build on, including studios that compete with your own, is a different kind of position entirely.

Unity has been here before with developer trust. In September 2023 it announced a Runtime Fee that charged studios per install, and the backlash was fierce enough that CEO John Riccitiello stepped down within weeks. The fee was scrapped completely in September 2024, and current CEO Matthew Bromberg later admitted Unity had been “practically at war with our customers”. A leveraged buyout means debt, and debt has to be paid from somewhere. Developers are going to want to know where.

Right now, none of that is more than speculation. There are talks, an investment bank, and a number somewhere north of where the stock was trading. Studios will be watching to see which of those three moves first.

#4385. For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise

For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight. But growing scientific evidence suggests that full-fat dairy may not carry the health risks many have come to expect.

A new Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence. Researchers found that adults who consumed three servings of full-fat dairy each day for 12 weeks did not experience harmful changes in body weight, body composition, energy metabolism, or blood cholesterol levels compared with participants following a diet containing little dairy.

Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy showed improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several important nutrients.

The findings, published in The Journal of Nutrition, raise new questions about longstanding dietary recommendations and suggest that the health effects of dairy may be more complicated than its saturated fat content alone would indicate.

For decades, nutrition guidelines in Canada and many other countries have recommended choosing low-fat or fat-free milk, yogurt, and other dairy products. The main concern has been saturated fat, which can raise levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood.

Often called "bad" cholesterol, LDL can contribute to fatty deposits in the arteries. Over time, this buildup can increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and other cardiovascular problems.

Because full-fat dairy contains more saturated fat than reduced-fat alternatives, health authorities have traditionally encouraged people to limit their intake.

However, research examining what happens when people actually consume full-fat dairy has produced a more complicated picture.

Anderson, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto's Temerty Faculty of Medicine, points out that numerous studies involving humans have failed to find a clear association between full-fat dairy consumption and poor health outcomes.

Other research has even identified potential protective effects. That includes a recent study led by Temerty Medicine professor Kozeta Milliku, which found an association between whole-fat milk consumption and a lower risk of childhood obesity.

These findings have prompted scientists to investigate whether dairy foods behave differently in the body than their individual nutrients might suggest.

What Happened When Adults Ate Full-Fat Dairy Every Day?

To explore the question, Anderson and his colleagues conducted a 12-week study involving 74 adults with overweight or obesity.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three dietary approaches. The first group followed a calorie-restricted diet containing little dairy. The second consumed three daily servings of dairy while maintaining an energy-neutral diet, meaning their calorie intake was intended to match the energy their bodies used. The third also consumed three servings of dairy each day but otherwise ate without specific calorie restrictions.

All participants received guidance based on Canada's food guide, and the researchers supplied full-fat dairy products during the study.

At the end of 12 weeks, the team compared several measures of metabolic health, including body weight, body composition, and cholesterol levels.

The results challenged expectations. Participants who consumed three servings of dairy daily did not show meaningful differences in weight gain, body composition, or blood cholesterol compared with those who ate little dairy.

The higher-dairy groups also experienced improvements in blood pressure and consumed more calcium, protein, and vitamin D. These nutrients play essential roles in maintaining healthy bones, supporting muscle function, and regulating numerous processes throughout the body.

"Those that had three servings of dairy didn't have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance," says Anderson.

Blood lipids are fats and fat-like substances circulating in the bloodstream, including cholesterol and triglycerides. Insulin resistance occurs when the body's cells become less responsive to insulin, making it harder to regulate blood sugar and increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Although the results are encouraging, the study was relatively small and lasted only three months. Longer and larger studies are needed to determine whether the findings translate into lasting health benefits or changes in cardiovascular disease risk.

Why might full-fat dairy have different health effects than researchers would predict from its saturated fat content?

One possible explanation is the dairy matrix hypothesis, an idea that emphasizes how the physical structure of food influences the way the body processes its nutrients.

Rather than treating milk, cheese, or yogurt as simple collections of fat, protein, vitamins, and minerals, this theory considers how those components interact within the food itself.

"With dairy products, it's got two proteins -- casein and whey -- that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in," says Anderson.

Casein and whey are the two major types of protein found in milk. Both provide amino acids that the body uses to build and maintain tissues, but they are digested and absorbed at different rates.

According to Anderson, the complex arrangement of proteins, fats, and other nutrients in dairy products can help regulate how quickly those nutrients are released during digestion.

This means the body's response to eating a whole dairy food may differ from its response to consuming an equivalent amount of saturated fat on its own.

The broader implication is that a food's health effects cannot always be predicted by examining a single ingredient. Its structure, nutritional composition, and interactions among nutrients may all matter.

Why the Findings Could Be Important for Older Adults

The researchers believe these results could be particularly relevant for older people, who often need to obtain sufficient protein and essential nutrients while consuming fewer calories.

As people age, their overall energy requirements frequently decrease. However, maintaining muscle mass, bone strength, and other important bodily functions still requires adequate nutrition.

That can make it difficult to meet nutritional needs, particularly for people with smaller appetites.

Anderson explains that dairy products offer a familiar, convenient source of concentrated nutrition. They provide protein, calcium, and other nutrients in foods that many older adults already enjoy and regularly consume.

The new findings suggest that including full-fat dairy in a balanced diet may help people meet these nutritional requirements without necessarily worsening cholesterol levels or markers associated with diabetes risk.

However, the study did not directly establish whether long-term consumption prevents or increases diabetes, heart disease, or other chronic conditions.

Rethinking Nutrition Advice Beyond Individual Nutrients

Beyond the debate over dairy fat, the research highlights a broader challenge in nutrition science: judging the health effects of entire foods rather than focusing exclusively on individual nutrients.

Traditional dietary advice has often emphasized reducing specific components, such as saturated fat. Although these recommendations are grounded in evidence about cardiovascular risk, researchers increasingly recognize that different foods containing the same nutrients may not have identical effects on health.

The University of Toronto findings contribute to this discussion by showing that full-fat dairy can be incorporated into certain diets without the unfavorable short-term metabolic changes that might be expected from its saturated fat content.

That does not mean saturated fat is harmless or that everyone should switch to full-fat dairy. Instead, it suggests that the overall food, its nutritional structure, and the broader dietary pattern deserve consideration.

For people trying to navigate changing nutrition recommendations and conflicting health messages, Anderson favors a practical approach rather than complicated dietary rules.

"Keep it simple, eat a variety of foods and not too much of anything."

This research was supported by Dairy Research Cluster 3 under the Canadian Agricultural Partnership AgriScience Program, and the Mitacs Accelerate program.

#4383. Battlefield 6 streamlines some of the most annoying Challenges yet again, takes out a few of them entirely

The easier and more accessible Battlefield Studios makes those Battlefield 6 Challenges, the better.

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a new patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

The Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The issue encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing new Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

#4382. Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk

Your daily cup of coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up in the morning. A long-running study of U.S. adults suggests that drinking caffeinated coffee regularly is associated with a substantially lower risk of dementia and better cognitive health as people age.

Researchers found that adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee developed dementia at considerably lower rates than those who rarely or never drank it. The findings were based on follow-up periods extending as long as 43 years, offering a valuable look at how everyday drinking habits relate to brain health over time.

The strongest associations appeared among people who drank two to three cups of caffeinated coffee each day. Tea consumption was also linked to better cognitive outcomes, although the amount associated with the greatest benefit was somewhat lower.

Interestingly, decaffeinated coffee did not show the same benefits, raising questions about whether caffeine itself might help explain the connection.

Coffee Drinkers Showed Much Lower Dementia Rates

One of the most striking findings involved the difference in dementia rates between regular coffee drinkers and people who consumed little or no coffee.

Among U.S. adults who drank higher amounts of caffeinated coffee, researchers recorded 141 dementia cases annually for every 100,000 people. In comparison, the rate was 330 cases per 100,000 people each year among those who rarely or never drank caffeinated coffee.

Dementia is a general term for conditions that progressively interfere with memory, thinking, reasoning, and the ability to perform everyday activities. Alzheimer's disease is its most common cause, although several other brain disorders can also lead to dementia.

While occasional forgetfulness can be a normal part of aging, dementia involves cognitive difficulties severe enough to disrupt daily life. Identifying lifestyle habits associated with lower dementia risk is therefore an important area of research, particularly as populations grow older.

The findings suggest that regular caffeinated coffee consumption may be one such habit. However, the results show an association rather than proving that coffee directly prevents dementia. Other differences between coffee drinkers and people who avoid coffee could also contribute to the observed results.

Coffee Was Also Linked to Better Cognitive Health

The potential benefits were not limited to diagnosed dementia. Participants who drank more caffeinated coffee were also less likely to report that their memory or thinking abilities had declined.

Researchers found that 7.8% of adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee reported subjective cognitive decline, compared with 9.5% of those who rarely or never drank it.

Subjective cognitive decline refers to changes in memory or thinking that people notice themselves, even when those difficulties have not necessarily been confirmed by formal cognitive testing. Someone experiencing it might feel that remembering information, concentrating, or finding the right words has become more difficult.

Such complaints do not automatically indicate dementia. Nevertheless, they can provide useful information about how people perceive changes in their cognitive abilities as they grow older.

The lower percentage among caffeinated coffee drinkers adds to the evidence linking coffee consumption with healthier cognitive aging.

How Much Coffee Offers the Greatest Benefit?

The researchers also examined whether the amount of coffee consumed was related to the strength of the observed benefits.

Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee per day was associated with the most favorable outcomes for dementia risk and cognitive functioning.

Notably, this association remained apparent regardless of participants' genetic risk of developing dementia. In other words, the relationship between coffee consumption and brain health was observed even among people whose inherited characteristics might make them more vulnerable to the disease.

Genetic risk refers to the influence of inherited variations in DNA that can increase or decrease a person's likelihood of developing certain conditions. Although genetics can play an important role in dementia, they are only one part of a much larger picture that includes age, general health, and lifestyle.

The results also suggest that drinking larger amounts of coffee is not necessarily better. Consumption beyond the range associated with the strongest benefits did not appear to provide additional protection.

Tea Drinkers May Benefit Too, but Decaf Was Different

Coffee was not the only beverage associated with better brain health. Researchers found that drinking tea was also linked to lower dementia risk and better cognitive functioning.

For tea, the strongest associations appeared among participants who consumed one to two cups per day. As with coffee, drinking more than this amount did not appear to produce further benefits.

However, the study did not distinguish between caffeinated and noncaffeinated tea. As a result, the findings cannot establish whether caffeine was responsible for the association observed among tea drinkers.

The results for coffee offered an additional clue. While regular caffeinated coffee was associated with lower dementia risk and better cognitive outcomes, decaffeinated coffee did not demonstrate the same benefits.

Caffeine is a naturally occurring stimulant found in coffee, tea, and several other plants. It acts on the central nervous system and is best known for temporarily increasing alertness and reducing feelings of tiredness.

Whether caffeine also contributes to better brain health over many years is a separate question. The difference between regular and decaffeinated coffee makes this possibility worth investigating, but it does not establish caffeine as the cause of the observed benefits.

Taken together, the findings suggest that moderate consumption of caffeinated coffee and tea may be associated with healthier brain aging. For coffee drinkers, two to three cups daily appeared to offer the strongest association, while one to two cups of tea showed the most favorable results among tea drinkers.

Although additional research is needed to determine whether these beverages directly influence dementia risk, the long-term findings offer encouraging news for people who already enjoy coffee or tea as part of their daily routine.

Materials provided by American Physiological Society. Original written by Tori DeAngelis. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
